item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Complication rates of emergency physician-performed regional anesthesia in emergency department and inpatient settings: a retrospective cohort study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Regional anesthesia is increasingly used in emergency departments (EDs) for acute pain management and procedural analgesia. Prior literature has demonstrated that ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia performed by emergency physicians (EPs) can provide effective analgesia while reducing opioid utilization and procedural sedation requirements. Although existing evidence supports the safety of EP-performed regional anesthesia in ED settings, limited data evaluate its use among hospitalized inpatients. Known complications of regional anesthesia include bleeding, infection, nerve injury, and local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), a rare but potentially life-threatening adverse event.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult patients undergoing EP-performed regional anesthesia between August 2022 and April 2026 at a tertiary care center. Patients were identified through electronic health record query and confirmed through manual chart review. Digital nerve blocks, dorsal penile blocks, trigger point injections, hematoma blocks, facial blocks, and dental blocks were excluded. The primary outcome was the occurrence of documented complications, including LAST, infection, clinically significant bleeding, or nerve injury.

Results: A total of 603 nerve blocks were included: 438 (72.6%) were performed in ED patients and 165 (27.4%) in inpatients. One possible case of LAST occurred (0.17%, 95% CI 0.004-0.92%). Cardiovascular deterioration occurred approximately six hours after block placement, with several competing explanations for the event. No infections, clinically significant bleeding complications, or nerve injuries were documented during the available follow-up. The two-sided exact 95% confidence interval for each zero-event outcome was 0%-0.61%.

Conclusion: Few complications were documented following emergency physician-performed regional anesthesia in ED and inpatient settings. These single-center findings are reassuring but do not exclude rare or delayed adverse events; larger studies with standardized follow-up are needed.

item.title: Resuscitation: Coronary artery disease severity in patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: a secondary analysis of the INCEPTION trial
item.description:
Background: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) can restore circulation in patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Subsequent invasive coronary angiography (ICA) allows the treatment of reversible causes and enables the evaluation of the presence and severity of coronary artery disease, facilitating insights into the cause of refractory arrest.

Methods: This secondary analysis of the INCEPTION trial, which randomized refractory OHCA patients between ECPR or conventional CPR, included all patients who underwent ICA. Angiograms were reanalyzed following a standardized protocol by two cardiologists, on presence of significant stenoses (>50%), with calculation of the SYNTAX score as a proxy for coronary artery disease severity. Patients were grouped as having "ROSC" or "no-ROSC", irrespective of the original assignment. In addition, patients with "no-ROSC" who had persistent ventricular arrhythmias were compared with those who converted to non-shockable rhythms.

Results: We included 73 patients: 29 ROSC and 44 no-ROSC (persistent ventricular arrhythmia, n=10; non-shockable conversion, n=34). No-ROSC patients had more frequent obstructive coronary artery disease (84% versus 66%, p=0.037), were more likely to have at least one acute culprit lesion (52% versus 21%, p=0.009) than ROSC patients, and had a higher SYNTAX score (17 ± 11 versus 10± 9, p=0.002). Lesions were predominantly left-sided.

Conclusion: Patients who do not achieve ROSC after refractory OHCA have more complex CAD and present more frequently with obstructive disease and a culprit lesion than patients who achieve ROSC. This seems particularly evident in patients who rapidly convert to a non-shockable rhythm.

item.title: Resuscitation: Prevalence and Patterns of Acute Cerebral Infarctions in Comatose Survivors of Cardiac Arrest
item.description:
Background: It is well-established that hypoxic-ischemic brain injury (HIBI) is the leading cause of death and disability after cardiac arrest. However, there is limited information about concurrent acute cerebral infarctions (ACI) and their association with clinical outcomes in comatose cardiac arrest survivors.

Methods: This was a retrospective multicenter cohort study of adult patients after cardiac arrest. We included patients who had brain MRIs performed within 7 days of cardiac arrest and excluded patients with a diagnosis of acute traumatic brain injury, intracranial hemorrhage, and acute ischemic stroke on admission. Univariate and multivariable analyses were performed to identify factors associated with ACI and to evaluate the association between ACI and unfavorable outcomes at hospital discharge (i.e., Cerebral Performance Category of 3-5).

Results: Of 351 patients included, 106 (30.2%) had ACI on MRI. The most common ACI pattern was multifocal small embolic-appearing (38.7%), followed by punctate (33%), territorial (18.9%), watershed (14.2%), and lacunar (14.2%), with overlapping patterns in 17% of patients with ACI. The patients with ACI were older (64 [54-71] vs 56 [39-66] years). Chronic white matter lesions were associated with ACI (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.79 [1.04-3.1], p<0.05). On univariate and multivariable analyses, ACI was not associated with unfavorable outcomes. Older age (aOR 1.04 [1.02-1.07], p<0.001) and presence of HIBI on MRI (aOR 8.41 [3.95-17.88], p<0.001) were associated with unfavorable outcomes on multivariable analysis.

Conclusions: ACI was present in nearly a third of patients with cardiac arrest. The most common pattern of ACI was multifocal embolic-appearing, and ACI was associated with chronic white matter lesions. The independent impact of ACI on cardiac arrest survivors' outcomes requires additional investigation in future prospective studies.

item.title: Resuscitation: Trends in Temperature Control after Cardiac Arrest in Cardiac Intensive Care Units: An Analysis from the Critical Care Cardiology Trials Network
item.description:
Introduction: Temperature control (TC) is recommended for comatose patients after cardiac arrest (CA). In the TTM2 trial, targeted normothermia (≤37.5°C) resulted in similar mortality and functional outcomes as targeted hypothermia (33°C).

Methods: The Critical Care Cardiology Trials Network (CCCTN) is a multinational registry of cardiac intensive care units (CICU) coordinated by the TIMI Study Group (Boston, MA). Between 2018-2024, consecutive comatose CA admissions were classified as occurring before vs. after publication and initial assimilation of TTM2. We compared temporal trends in TC use, temperature targets, and outcomes between the pre- and post-TTM2 eras, including in subgroups with initial shockable (VT/VF) vs. non-shockable (PEA/asystole) rhythms. Multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for baseline differences.

Results: Among 1,706 comatose CA admissions, 773 occurred in the pre-TTM2 era and 933 in the post-TTM2 era. TC use was similar pre- and post-TTM2 (74% vs. 78%; p=0.06), including in subgroups with shockable (84% vs. 85%; p=0.85) and non-shockable rhythms (64% vs. 68%; p=0.26). Post-TTM2, target temperatures shifted towards normothermia (target temperature ≥36°C: 38% [pre] vs. 71% [post]; p<0.001). Mortality was higher post-TTM2 vs. pre-TTM2 among CA admissions with shockable rhythms (50% vs. 42%; aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.11-1.99), but not with non-shockable rhythms (76% vs. 75%; aOR 1.03 [0.71-1.49]). Comparing CA admissions with shockable rhythms to non-CA admissions, the difference in proportional increase in mortality between eras was not statistically significant (ROR 1.20 [0.91-1.58]).

Conclusion: In a large CICU cohort of comatose CA patients, overall use of TC remained stable over the study period (2018-2024), but clinicians increasingly favored targeted normothermia. In-hospital mortality among patients with initial shockable rhythms was higher in the post-TTM2 era, which may be related to secular changes in CICU patients over time.

item.title: Resuscitation: Psychological outcomes of spouses of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors according to witnessing and cardiopulmonary resuscitation performance: Results from the cross-sectional DANCAS study
item.description:
Aim: Spouses often witness out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) and perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), but associations with psychological outcomes remain unclear. The aim was to describe the prevalence of symptoms of anxiety, depression and caregiver strain according to spouses' level of involvement and to investigate associations between involvement and these outcomes.

Methods: This cross-sectional study used data from spouses participating in the national DANCAS survey. Symptoms of anxiety and depression were assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and caregiver strain using the Modified Caregiver Strain Index. Associations between involvement and psychological outcomes were investigated using logistic regression models adjusted for sex, age and employment status.

Results: Of 461 spouses, 32% (n=148) reported symptoms of anxiety, 10% (n=44) symptoms of depression and 25% (n=115) caregiver strain. The prevalence of symptoms did not differ significantly across the levels of involvement. In adjusted analyses, witnessing OHCA without performing CPR was associated with higher odds of symptoms of depression compared with not witnessing OHCA (OR 3.18 95% CI 1.38-7.35). No statistically significant associations were observed for symptoms of anxiety or caregiver strain.

Conclusion: Symptoms of anxiety and caregiver strain were common across all levels of involvement. Witnessing OHCA without performing CPR was associated with higher odds of symptoms of depression, while no other associations were found. These findings suggest that level of involvement alone may be insufficient to identify spouses at risk of psychological distress.

item.title: Resuscitation: Sex Differences in Neurological Outcomes After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Sequential Adjusted Analysis from the JAAM Registry
item.description:
Introduction: Sex differences in outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain controversial. We examined sex differences in neurological outcomes after OHCA and explored how the estimated association changed as measured patient, arrest, and treatment characteristics were sequentially included.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using data from the Japan Association for Acute Medicine OHCA Registry (2014-2022). Adult non-traumatic OHCA patients (≥ 18) were included. The primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2) at 1 month, and the secondary outcome was 1-month survival. Sequential logistic regression models adjusted for age, arrest characteristics, bystander interventions, initial shockable rhythm, public-access automated external defibrillator (PAD/AED) use, and advanced treatments. Age-stratified post hoc analyses further evaluated PAD/AED use and initial rhythm.

Results: Among 65,346 patients (39,576 men and 25,770 women), women had lower crude 1-month favorable neurological outcomes (2.4% vs. 5.4%; p < 0.01) and 1-month survival (4.5% vs. 8.7%; p < 0.01). The crude odds ratio (OR) for 1-month favorable neurological outcome in women versus men was 0.44 (95% CI, 0.40-0.48), compared with 1.00 (95% CI, 0.89-1.12) in the fully adjusted model. Women aged 18-64 years had better neurological outcomes than men when PAD/AED was used (66.7% vs. 49.0%; p < 0.01) or when the initial rhythm was shockable (37.7% vs. 30.0%; p < 0.01), but these differences diminished with age.

Conclusions: Women have poorer crude neurological and survival outcomes after OHCA. However, the association between women and favorable neurological outcomes progressively attenuated with the sequential inclusion of measured factors. The causal contributions of individual factors cannot be determined from this exploratory sequential analysis.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Modified Cunningham technique compared with the standard Cunningham technique for acute anterior shoulder dislocation: a prospective randomized study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: Acute anterior shoulder dislocation is a painful condition that usually needs rapid reduction in the emergency department. The Standard Cunningham technique (SCT) is a single-clinician, medication-free method built on relaxation of shoulder girdle muscle spasm, but reported first-method success and procedure duration vary across studies. We evaluated whether a Modified Cunningham technique (MCT) improved reduction success and reduced procedure time without increasing pain or complications.

Methods: We performed a prospective, randomized, parallel-group trial in two tertiary emergency medicine clinics. Adults with acute anterior shoulder dislocation were randomized in equal numbers to SCT or MCT (32 patients in each group). The assigned maneuver was attempted once and stopped at 10 min if reduction had not occurred. No intravenous line, sedative, or analgesic was used before the assigned attempt. Successful reduction with the allocated maneuver was the sole primary outcome. Reduction time, intra-reduction Visual Analog Scale (VAS) score, and procedure-related complications were secondary outcomes.

Results: The assigned maneuver reduced the shoulder in 28/32 patients (87.5%) in the MCT group and in 20/32 patients (62.5%) in the SCT group (Fisher exact p = 0.041; OR = 4.20, 95% CI: 1.18-14.94). After exploratory adjustment for sex and prior dislocation, MCT remained associated with higher odds of successful reduction (adjusted OR = 4.21, 95% CI: 1.14-15.54; p = 0.031). Among successful reductions, median reduction time was 220.0 s (IQR 187.5-248.8) with MCT and 347.5 s (IQR 217.5-525.0) with SCT (p = 0.005). No successful reduction exceeded the prespecified 600-s treatment period. Pain scores during reduction were similar (p = 0.107), and no complications occurred.

Conclusion: MCT increased first-attempt success and shortened reduction time compared with SCT in adults with anterior shoulder dislocation. Because pain scores were comparable and no adverse events were observed, MCT may be considered a rapid, practical, medication-free option for emergency department reduction.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Sepsis response team architecture in the emergency department: A systematic review of process reliability and patient outcomes
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Implementation gaps in emergency departments remain substantial despite widespread dissemination of evidence-based sepsis bundles. Early recognition and timely initiation of evidence-based interventions while engaging front line staff are critical to improving outcomes, yet the contribution of organized sepsis response teams remains incompletely understood.

Objective: To evaluate the impact of sepsis teams on the four main items of sepsis bundle compliance in the ED and clinical outcomes of sepsis patients.

Methods: A systematic review done according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines was conductedincluding studies between 2010 and 2025 that evaluated team organizational interventions in adult emergency department settings. The searches were performed in PubMed, Cochrane Library (CENTRAL), Scopus, and CINAHL databases, supplemented by gray literature sources. The primary outcome was adherence to the sepsis bundle (lactate measurement, blood culture, antibiotic administration, fluid resuscitation). Secondary outcomes include length of stay, hospital and ICU mortality and resource utilization. A qualitative narrative synthesis was adopted given heterogeneity in study designs.

Results: 19 studies met the inclusion criteria. Interventions were grouped inductively in four categories based on 1) sepsis identification; 2) team activation; 3) task delegation, and 4) treatment delivery. Sepsis response teams and nurse-driven protocols were associated with improved bundle adherence and shorter time to antibiotics, particularly in settings with low baseline compliance. Effects on clinical outcomes such as mortality, ICU admission, and length of stay were inconsistent across studies. There was no data on the long-term sustainability of teams' training and impact on the outcomes.

Conclusions: Sepsis response teams appear to improve the reliability and timeliness of evidence-based care, especially in lactate measurement, blood cultures, antibiotics, and fluids. However, the effects on mortality, ICU admission, length of stay, and costs are inconsistent, maybe due to large variations in team composition, activation criteria, authority, training, and sustainability. Future studies should preferentially adopt the Sepsis-3 definitions, and include a clear description of the team, and evaluate impacts by severity.

item.title: Crit Care: Cholesterol sulfate as a novel theranostic target for sepsis-induced liver injury through Beclin1-mediated autophagy enhancement and pyroptosis suppression
item.description:
Background: Sepsis remains a life-threatening syndrome, and septic liver injury is a frequent and critical complication for which no specific pharmacological therapy exists. Current biomarkers lack sufficient specificity for early diagnosis and severity assessment, highlighting an urgent need for novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

Objective: To identify key metabolites involved in sepsis pathogenesis and to evaluate the diagnostic and therapeutic potential of cholesterol sulfate (CS) in sepsis-induced liver injury, as well as to elucidate the underlying molecular mechanisms.

Methods: We performed transcriptomic (GSE65682) and metabolomic (SepsisLiMetDB) screens sequentially and independently to identify sepsis-associated metabolites. The functional role of CS was evaluated in cecal ligation and puncture (CLP) mouse model using both exogenous CS supplementation and Sult2b1 genetic knockout approaches, as well as in vitro using primary hepatocytes and AML12 cells. The underlying molecular mechanisms were explored via molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, cellular thermal shift assay, co-immunoprecipitation, MDC staining, GFP-LC3/LysoTracker Red co-localization, ROS detection, and pyroptosis marker analysis in AML12 cells with or without Beclin1 knockdown. Therapeutic efficacy was compared with clinically used agents (reduning and ulinastatin) in a mouse endotoxemia model. Diagnostic potential was assessed in independent bacterial sepsis (n = 114) and COVID-19 (n = 43) cohorts.

Results: Through unbiased multi-omics screening, we identified CS as one of the most markedly depleted metabolites in sepsis. Sult2b1-deficient mice lacking endogenous CS showed exacerbated systemic inflammation, aggravated liver injury, and mortality-all of which were significantly reversed by exogenous CS supplementation. Mechanistically, CS directly bound Beclin1, suppressed its ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, enhanced autophagic flux, and attenuated oxidative stress and GSDMD-mediated pyroptosis. Notably, CS exhibited superior efficacy to Reduning and comparable therapeutic effects to Ulinastatin. Clinically, reduced circulating CS levels correlated with both bacterial and viral sepsis and with disease severity, supporting its potential diagnostic value.

Conclusions: Our study establishes, for the first time, CS as a functionally protective metabolite in sepsis, with therapeutic efficacy superior to existing clinical agents, and identify circulating CS as a potential diagnostic biomarker for sepsis and disease severity.

item.title: Resuscitation: Opioid administration prior to in-hospital cardiac arrest
item.description:
Background: Opioid administration is common in hospitalised patients. The opioid antagonist naloxone has been proposed as a potential adjunct during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. We aimed to describe opioid exposure within 24 hours before in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) and explore associations with outcomes.

Methods: Retrospective observational study on all adult (≥18 years) IHCA during 2024 across nine hospitals in southernmost Sweden, registered in the Swedish Registry for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation. Opioid administrations were collected from medical records. Exploratory logistic regressions assessed associations between opioid exposure (any administration and cumulative dose) and return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and 30-day survival, adjusted for age, sex, witnessed IHCA and national early warning score.

Results: Opioids were administered within 24 hours preceding IHCA in 108/267 (40%) patients and in 43/267 (16%) patients within the last two hours. Median time from last opioid administration to IHCA was 2.7 hours (IQR 0.5-7.7). Median oral cumulative morphine milligram equivalent dose was 17 mg (IQR 9-30). Naloxone was administered in 6/267 (2%) of IHCA. Opioid administration within 24 hours prior to IHCA was not associated with ROSC (OR 1.03 [95%CI 0.59-1.78, p=0.93]) or 30-day survival (OR 0.98 [95%CI 0.55-1.73], p=0.94). Higher cumulative opioid doses were associated with lower odds of ROSC (OR 0.91 [95%CI 0.83-1.00], p=0.042), but not 30-day survival (OR 0.98 [95%CI 0.90-1.08], p=0.69).

Conclusions: Opioid administration within 24 hours preceding IHCA is common, with frequent administrations shortly before cardiac arrest. Further research is warranted investigating a potential role of opioid reversal during IHCA.

item.title: Resuscitation: MRI-Derived Spatial Patterns of Post-Cardiac Arrest Brain Injury Are Associated With Cerebral Oxygenation Dynamics
item.description:
Introduction: Post-cardiac arrest brain injury (PCABI) varies substantially in severity and anatomical distribution between patients. We evaluated whether anatomically resolved diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) lesion patterns are associated with cerebral oxygenation following cardiac arrest.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective study of 24 patients with PCABI who underwent brain MRI and intraparenchymal neuromonitoring. Ischemic lesion burden was quantified as the percentage of tissue with an apparent diffusion coefficient <650×10-6 mm2/s across 164 brain segments. Principal component analysis (PCA) and k-means clustering were used to identify MRI-derived injury patterns for downstream physiological analysis. Brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO2), intracranial pressure (ICP), and jugular venous oxygen saturation (SjvO2) were analyzed during the first 72 hours after cardiac arrest.

Results: Three reproducible MRI-derived injury patterns (i.e., clusters) were identified (n=13, 6, and 5), with progressively greater whole-brain lesion burden from Cluster 1 (10.16% [9.00-11.68]) to Cluster 2 (22.14% [17.83-25.12]) and Cluster 3 (38.40% [30.92-41.45]; p<0.001). Greater whole-brain lesion burden was associated with lower PbtO2 (r=-0.44, p=0.031) and higher SjvO2 (r=0.53, p=0.009), but not ICP (r=0.11, p=0.623). PbtO2 was lower in Cluster 3 than Cluster 1 (16.0±10.6 vs 26.6±9.0 mmHg; p=0.027), whereas SjvO2 was higher in Clusters 2 and 3 than Cluster 1 (both p<0.05).

Discussion: MRI-derived injury patterns differed in global lesion burden, PbtO2, and SjvO2, but not ICP. Greater whole-brain lesion burden was associated with lower PbtO2 and higher SjvO2, whereas no association was observed with ICP. These findings show that the extent and distribution of diffusion-restricted brain injury are linked to distinct cerebral oxygenation profiles after cardiac arrest.

item.title: Resuscitation: Reversed airflow during asynchronous volume controlled mechanical ventilation in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: a physiological observational study
item.description:
Aim: Chest compressions during the inspiratory phase of a ventilation can force air out of the lungs, so-called reversed airflow. Human data on this phenomenon during mechanical ventilation are lacking. We aimed to quantify its frequency and magnitude during asynchronous mechanical ventilation in intubated adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients receiving continuous chest compressions.

Methods: This single-centre descriptive cross-sectional study used prospectively collected data from patients treated by a physician-staffed prehospital team. After tracheal intubation, patients were ventilated with an Oxylog 3000 transport ventilator in volume-controlled mode without positive end-expiratory pressure, during continuous manual chest compressions. Intratracheal pressures recorded via two catheters allowed calculation of airflow and ventilation parameters during the first minute after intubation. Reversed airflow was defined as expiratory airflow during the inspiratory phase of a mechanical breath. Continuous data are reported as median (first-third quartile).

Results: Twelve patients were included (median age 68 years [62-75]; 7 [58.3%] male), of whom 5 (41.7%) achieved sustained return of spontaneous circulation. Reversed airflow occurred in 10 (83.3%; 95% CI 55.2-95.3) patients and in 141 of 172 (82.0%; 95% CI 75.6-87.0) analysed ventilations. The median reversed-airflow volume was 61 mL [42-80] per episode. Median ventilation rate was 14 breaths/min [13-16], gross inspiratory tidal volume 324 mL [305-345], minute ventilation 4.8 L/min [3.8-5.9], and peak inspiratory pressure 46 cmH2O [40-52].

Conclusion: Reversed airflow occurred frequently during asynchronous volume-controlled mechanical ventilation with the Oxylog 3000 in intubated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients receiving continuous manual chest compressions. Its physiological and clinical implications require further investigation.

item.title: Resuscitation: Improvement in Peak Oxygen Consumption Following Cardiac Rehabilitation in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (OHCA) Survivors: A Comparative Study with ST-elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) Patients
item.description:
Aim: To investigate the impact of phase II cardiac rehabilitation (CR) on cardiopulmonary fitness in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survivors and to compare outcomes with ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) patients categorized by Killip classification.

Methods: This retrospective study was conducted at a tertiary medical center in Taiwan. We included 31 OHCA survivors whose cardiac events occurred between February 1, 2012, and June 30, 2023, and who completed phase II CR with symptom-limited cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) performed before and after CR. For comparison, 78 patients with STEMI were included, comprising 54 with Killip class I-II and 24 with Killip class III-IV. All participants underwent phase II CR, which was scheduled for 36 sessions and consisted of aerobic and resistance training. The primary outcomes were changes in CPET parameters after CR, including peak workload, peak oxygen consumption (V̇O2peak), and percent-predicted V̇O2peak. Paired t tests were used to evaluate within-group changes, and repeated-measures ANOVA was employed to compare between-group differences.

Results: OHCA survivors exhibited significant improvements in V̇O2peak (+3.9 mL/kg/min, p < 0.001), peak workload, and percent-predicted V̇O2peak after CR, with a mean improvement of 24.8% in V̇O2peak. These gains were comparable to those seen in STEMI patients across Killip classes. Although OHCA survivors had lower pre-CR V̇O2peak, they demonstrated similar trainability.

Conclusions: This study highlights that OHCA survivors can undergo CR and achieve meaningful improvements in cardiopulmonary fitness, comparable to patients with myocardial infarction. These findings support the implementation of structured CR programs in this high-risk population.

item.title: Chest: Delayed oxygen saturation recovery after the 6-minute walk test: Prognostic implications for COPD patients
item.description:
Research question: The 6-minute walk test (6MWT) is a fundamental instrument in the clinical management of COPD patients, yet the prognostic value of specific physiological parameters during the recovery phase remains underexplored. This study aimed to determine whether the recovery time of oxygen saturation (SpO2-RT) following a 6MWT is associated with long-term prognosis (death and hospitalizations) in a cohort of patients with COPD.

Study design and methods: In this prospective observational cohort, 512 consecutive patients were recruited through the Galdakao University Hospital Respiratory Service and underwent pulmonary function and quadriceps strength assessments, multisensor accelerometry, and a 6MWT. Desaturation was defined as a ≥3% decrease in SpO2 from baseline during the 6MWT; SpO2-RT was the time from test completion until SpO2 returned to baseline.

Results: Of the 512 enrolled patients 25% were female. Those who experienced oxygen desaturation during the 6MWT exhibited significantly worse pulmonary function (FEV1%, RV%, IC/TLC and DLCO%) (p <.0001), higher fibrinogen levels (p =.01), lower quadriceps strength (p =.02), reduced PA (p <.0001), and a shorter distance walked (p <.0001). Within the desaturation sub-cohort, differences were analysed based on a SpO2-RT cut-off ≥ 80 seconds. Patients with a prolonged SpO2-RT exhibited more severe pulmonary function impairment (p values ranging from .02 to <.0001), significantly lower PA (p =.001), and shorter distance 6MWT (p <.0001). During the 3-year follow-up increased SpO2-RT was associated with increased mortality (p =.03) and hospitalizations (p =.0003). In the adjusted analyses, prolonged SpO2-RT was associated with an approximately twofold higher risk of both hospitalization (p = .02) and mortality (p =.04).

Interpretation: A prolonged SpO2-RT ≥ 80 identifies a COPD phenotype characterized by diminished respiratory reserve and an increased risk of subsequent exacerbation-related hospitalizations and all-cause mortality. SpO2-RT is a simple, accessible metric that enhances the prognostic utility of the standard 6MWT.

item.title: Chest: Respiratory Therapists' Intentions to Leave their Current Position
item.description:
Background: Many respiratory therapy departments face staffing shortages with high turnover rates. What drives turnover among respiratory therapists (RTs) is unclear.

Research question: What variables are associated with RT's intention to leave their current position.

Study design and methods: We performed a planned secondary analysis of a multicenter, multinational study of RT burnout. We compared those with an intent to leave score ≥ 50 to those with a score < 50 and report odds ratios OR with 95% confidence intervals (CI) using univariable logistic regression.

Results: We received 1,014 responses and 536 (53%) had an intention to leave score ≥ 50. Statistically significant factors associated with intention to leave included: emotional exhaustion (OR 13.2), felt other RTs were burned out (OR 6.4), felt their workload was too high (OR 3.9), exposure to incivility (OR 3.4), unable to complete all their work (OR 2.4), inadequate staffing (OR 2.3), activities restricted due to illness (OR 2.0), worked 31-50 hours in the ICU (OR 1.6), bachelor's degree (OR 1.4) and missed work for any reason (OR 1.4). Statistically significant factors associated with low intention to leave included: felt valued by their organization (OR 0.1), a positive leadership score (OR 0.2), agreed their director/manager cared about them as a person (OR 0.2), satisfaction with total compensation (OR 0.3), < 2 years as an RT (OR 0.4), and spending their time performing high value activities (OR 0.6).

Interpretation: Over half of RTs had an intention to leave. Emotional exhaustion, incivility, leadership, staffing, workload, hours worked in the ICU, bachelor's degree, and perceived value were all associated with intent to leave while hours worked, and patient population were not associated with intent to leave.

item.title: Lancet: Identifying which patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer benefit most from androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (STOPCAP): a systematic review and meta-analysis of individual participant data
item.description:
Background: Adding novel androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) to standard of care improves outcomes for patients with metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC), but whether benefits are consistent across patient subgroups remains uncertain. We aimed to assess whether ARPI effects vary according to participant or tumour characteristics, or by docetaxel use.

Methods: In this systematic review and meta-analysis (STOPCAP), we sought individual participant data for completed trials adding ARPIs to standard of care. Intention-to-treat, two-stage, common-effect meta-analysis of hazard ratios (HRs) were adjusted for a common set of covariates and docetaxel use. Main effects were based on overall survival. Interaction effects were based on progression-free survival (PFS) to maximise power, then overall survival whenever significant PFS interactions were found. Prostate cancer-specific survival (PCSS), exploratory competing risk analyses of causes of death, and 5-year absolute effects were estimated overall and for key subgroups.

Findings: Individual participant data were available from seven eligible trial comparisons (two comparisons from STAMPEDE, LATITUDE, PEACE-1, SWOG-S1216, ENZAMET, and TITAN) and 7778 participants (66% of total eligible). In the primary analysis of six trials (6467 participants and 3322 events), adding an ARPI improved overall survival (HR 0·66 [95% CI 0·62-0·710]; p<0·0001), with a 13% absolute improvement in 5-year survival. Similar results were observed for PFS. No evidence of effect variation was observed by ARPI class, docetaxel use, disease volume, Gleason score, performance status, or metastatic burden. ARPI effects on PFS varied by continuous age (interaction p=0·0005) and by age group (interaction p=0·0027), with patterns differing by ARPI class (biosynthesis versus receptor inhibitors: p=0·022) and similar results for overall survival. Based on individual participant data from three abiraterone trials (100% of eligible participants), effects on overall survival varied by age group (interaction p=0·0006), with an absolute 5-year improvement of about 15% for patients younger than 75 years but minimal benefit (about 1%) in those aged 75 years or older. Abiraterone improved 5-year PCSS across all age groups (11-18%), with a similar reduction in cumulative incidence of cancer deaths. However, in patients aged 75 years or older, abiraterone was associated with a 12% increase in 5-year cumulative incidence of non-cancer deaths. Based on limited individual participant data for receptor inhibitors (two trials; 35% of eligible participants), there was no clear evidence that effects on overall survival varied by age group (interaction p=0·078), and results from the STAMPEDE trial comparison of combined abiraterone and enzalutamide were similar.

Interpretation: Adding an ARPI to standard of care significantly improved overall survival for most patients with mHSPC. Although abiraterone improved cancer-specific survival for all, non-cancer mortality was increased among older patients. Further individual participant data are needed to fully assess the effects of androgen receptor inhibitors by age. Current data highlight the importance of considering age and comorbidities when selecting ARPI therapy.

item.title: Lancet: Envudeucitinib in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (ONWARD1 and ONWARD2): results from two replicate, multicentre, double-blinded, placebo-controlled and active comparator-controlled, phase 3 randomised controlled trials
item.description:
Background: Safe and highly effective oral treatment options for patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis are scarce. Here, we aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of envudeucitinib (ESK-001), an investigational next-generation, highly selective, oral, allosteric tyrosine kinase 2 inhibitor, in patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.

Methods: ONWARD1 (NCT06586112) and ONWARD2 (NCT06588738) are completed, replicate, multicentre, randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled and active comparator-controlled, phase 3 trials that enrolled patients in 333 sites (eg, research and medical centres, private practices, and hospitals) across 19 countries. Adults with a diagnosis of plaque psoriasis for at least 6 months, body surface area of at least 10%, and Psoriasis Area Severity Index (PASI) of at least 12 were randomly assigned 2:1:1 to oral envudeucitinib 40 mg twice daily, placebo, or apremilast 30 mg twice daily for 24 weeks of treatment. At week 16, patients receiving placebo were transitioned to envudeucitinib. Coprimary endpoints were at least 75% improvement from baseline in Psoriasis Area Severity Index (PASI 75) and static Physician's Global Assessment (sPGA) of 0 or 1 at week 16 (envudeucitinib vs placebo). Secondary endpoints were assessed at weeks 16 and 24 (envudeucitinib vs placebo and/or apremilast). Safety assessments included adverse events and laboratory parameters.

Findings: From July 25, 2024, to Dec 18, 2025, 912 and 859 patients were randomly assigned to ONWARD1 and ONWARD2, respectively (envudeucitinib, n=459 and n=433; placebo, n=230 and n=211; apremilast, n=223 and n=215). In both trials, coprimary and all key secondary endpoints were met (all p<0·0001). At week 16, envudeucitinib resulted in statistically significant PASI 75 responses versus placebo (ONWARD1: 351 [76·5%] of 459 vs 43 [18·7%] of 230; ONWARD2: 305 [70·4%] of 433 vs 29 [13·7%] of 211; both p<0·0001) and sPGA of 0 or 1 responses versus placebo (ONWARD1: 280 [61·0%] of 459 vs 23 [10·0%] of 230; ONWARD2: 248 [57·3%] of 433 vs 12 [5·7%] of 211; both p<0·0001). Up to week 16, 525 (59·0%) of 890 receiving envudeucitinib, 166 (37·6%) of 441 receiving placebo, and 224 (51·1%) of 438 patients receiving apremilast had one or more treatment-emergent adverse event. Up to week 24, 566 (63·6%) of 890 and 248 (56·6%) of 438 patients originally randomly assigned to envudeucitinib or apremilast had one or more treatment-emergent adverse event. Treatment-emergent adverse events were mostly mild or moderate and responsive to standard therapies; headache (97 [10·9%] of 890), nasopharyngitis (93 [10·4%] of 890), acne (60 [6·7%] of 890), and upper respiratory tract infection (57 [6·4%] of 890) occurred in at least 5% of patients receiving envudeucitinib during the trials. Up to week 16, serious adverse events occurred in 19 (2·1%) of 890 patients receiving envudeucitinib, five (1·1%) of 441 patients receiving placebo, and five (1·1%) of 438 patients receiving apremilast.

Interpretation: Envudeucitinib improved both skin signs and patient-reported outcomes, and maintained favourable tolerability, supporting its role as a promising oral treatment for patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Restaurant-related occupational injuries among workers' compensation claimants in North Carolina emergency departments, 2017-2024
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Restaurant workers experience a high burden of occupational injury, particularly cuts/lacerations, burns, and slips/falls. Updated surveillance is needed to describe restaurant-related occupational injuries among workers seeking emergency care.

Methods: North Carolina Disease Event Tracking and Epidemiologic Collection Tool (NC DETECT) emergency department (ED) visits from 2017 to 2024 were analyzed. Restaurant-related injuries were identified using ICD-10-CM code Y92.511 and restricted to visits listing workers' compensation as the expected payer. Annual rates per 100,000 restaurant workers were calculated. Injury characteristics were compared by sex and age using prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

Results: Overall, 654 ED visits were reported. Annual rates peaked in 2019 (36.0/100,000), declined through 2023, and increased slightly in 2024. Most injuries involved the upper extremity (59.5%) and resulted in open wounds (36.1%) or burns/corrosions (22.9%); common mechanisms included cut/pierce injuries (28.0%), contact with hot objects/substances (21.4%), and falls (20.6%). Compared with males, females had fewer open wounds (PR = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.42-0.64) and cut/pierce injuries (PR = 0.45, 95% CI: 0.35-0.59), but more falls (PR = 2.18, 95% CI: 1.56-3.05). Compared with workers aged 15-44 years, those aged ≥45 years had more falls (PR = 3.41, 95% CI: 2.57-4.53) and fractures (PR = 3.01, 95% CI: 1.83-4.95).

Conclusions: Restaurant-related occupational injuries commonly involved the upper extremity and were frequently associated with cuts/pierces, burns, and falls. Consistent with the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) Hierarchy of Controls, priorities could include engineering or equipment-based controls to reduce exposure to sharp instruments, hot surfaces and substances, and slipping hazards, alongside safe work practices and personal protective equipment.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Emotion regulation abilities among people who use electronic cigarettes, tobacco cigarettes, or both
item.description:
Background: Emotion regulation difficulties can hinder nicotine cessation. Although people who smoke tobacco cigarettes struggle to regulate negative emotions using cognitive reappraisal, whether people who use electronic cigarettes experience similar difficulties remains unknown. We therefore compared the cognitive reappraisal abilities of people who use electronic cigarettes on a daily basis, with the abilities of people who use tobacco cigarettes daily, people who use both products daily, and people who use neither.

Methods: Between March and September 2025, 53 people who use electronic cigarettes daily, 50 people who use tobacco cigarettes daily, 52 people who use both nicotine products daily and 50 people who use neither were all recruited through Prolific Academic and completed an online cognitive reappraisal task and the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), administered via Gorilla. Group differences in reappraisal success and DERS scores were examined using ANOVAs, while relationships with nicotine use behaviours were assessed using partial correlations. All analyses controlled for age, gender, alcohol use and cannabis use.

Results: People who use neither electronic or tobacco cigarettes exhibited greater reappraisal success than all three nicotine-using groups, which did not differ from one another. Further, greater self-reported electronic cigarette consumption was associated with poorer reappraisal success, whereas no such relationship was observed for daily tobacco cigarette use. Finally, there were no group effects on, or relationships between nicotine use and, DERS scores.

Conclusions: This study provides the first evidence that people who use electronic cigarettes show cognitive reappraisal difficulties comparable to those who use tobacco cigarettes. These findings may have implications for developing psychological interventions to support electronic cigarette cessation, although further research is required to establish their relevance to quitting outcomes.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Energy landscape analysis reveals constrained attractor dynamics linked to alcohol-use severity in alcohol use disorder
item.description:
Background: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) involves large-scale brain network dysregulation. However, conventional connectivity approaches provide limited insight into how the brain enters, maintains, and switches between functional states. We applied energy landscape analysis to characterize attractor-like dynamics in AUD.

Methods: We analyzed resting-state fMRI data from 93 individuals with AUD and 91 matched healthy control participants from the Human Connectome Project. Regional time series were summarized into eight functional systems and modeled using a pairwise maximum entropy model. We identified attractor-like states and quantified occupancy and transition rates. Group comparisons used false discovery rate correction; clinical relevance was assessed using partial correlation, moderation, and mediation analyses.

Results: The model identified six attractor-like states, including two primary states interpreted as putative sensory-attentional (B1) and affective-reward-related (B6) configurations based on their network profiles. AUD was associated with reduced bidirectional transitions between B1 and B6, reduced occupancy of B1 and B6, and greater occupancy of an intermediate state, B4. Exploratory AUD-only analyses showed nominal associations of lower B6 occupancy with more frequent heavy drinking and of reduced B1 occupancy and fewer B1-to-B6 transitions with greater recent weekend alcohol consumption. AUD status moderated the B1-to-B6 transition-weekend alcohol consumption relationship, and B1 occupancy partially accounted for associations between AUD status and recent drinking and alcohol dependence status.

Conclusions: Energy landscape analysis revealed constrained attractor dynamics in AUD, with reduced transition rates between putative sensory-attentional and affective-reward-related configurations and redistribution toward an intermediate state. These findings highlight the clinical relevance of altered state dynamics in AUD.

item.title: Crit Care: Thiamine-deficiency in the ICU-patient - When the plug is out
item.description:
There is a notorious difficulty in judging micronutrient stores and requirements in critically ill patients and deficiency states will be rarely associated with clinical symptoms. A fundamental exception is vitamin B1, thiamine, a micronutrient of crucial importance in mitochondrial energy production. With thiamine deficiency "the energy plug is out", resulting in multiple organ dysfunctions, such as of brain, heart, kidney or respiratory system, lactate formation is increased, lactate clearance reduced, all fundamentally affecting the course of disease and prognosis of a patient. Several patient groups, such as malnourished subjects or patients with liver or kidney disease are already deficient prior to hospital or ICU admission, but there is also a high risk of developing deficiency during ICU stay. There are several well defined patient groups at risk, however, there is no need to measure plasma concentrations, as assays are mostly not available, costly and actually do not reflect the cellular status. There is quite solid evidence that thiamine may preserve / improve organ function (brain, heart, kidney), reduce blood lactate concentration and reduce mortality in various groups of critically ill patient. An extra thiamine supplementation should be given in high-risk patient groups, which bears no risk of inducing toxicity and is cheap, so we advocate to administer thiamine whenever a deficiency state is suspected.

item.title: Chest: Epigenetic Aging and Severity of Nocturnal Intermittent Hypoxia
item.description:
Background: Nocturnal intermittent hypoxia (IH) is a hallmark feature of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and contributes to oxidative stress and inflammation, which in turn may accelerate biological aging. Epigenetic clocks can estimate biological age from DNA methylation (DNAm) patterns.

Research question: Is greater severity of IH associated with increased biological aging?

Study design and methods: We studied adults referred for suspected OSA in a multisite sleep and circadian research network, a cross-sectional observational cohort (2016-2021). IH severity was assessed using the 4% oxygen desaturation index (ODI) from home sleep apnea testing or in-laboratory polysomnography (PSG). DNAm from peripheral blood leukocytes was assayed using Illumina EPIC arrays. Epigenetic age acceleration (EAA) and pace of aging were calculated using multiple DNAm clocks. Linear regression models were adjusted for leukocyte composition, age, sex, ethnicity, BMI, smoking, site, alcohol, diabetes, and hypertension. A false discovery rate of 0.05 was used.

Results: A total of 1364 participants were included (median age, 56 yrs; median ODI, 16/h; median BMI, 32 kg/m2; 57% male). Higher ODI was associated with EAA for PhenoAge (β = 0.028, adjusted P = .0048) and with pace of aging (DunedinPACE, β = 0.0005, adjusted P =.0012). No significant associations were observed for first-generation clocks.

Interpretation: Greater IH severity, as assessed by ODI, was independently associated with increased biological aging as measured by PhenoAge and DunedinPACE clocks. These findings support a link between OSA and biological aging, raising the possibility of using epigenetic age measures as biomarkers of OSA-related morbidity.

item.title: Chest: DHEA-S in Pulmonary Hypertension: Insights from PVDOMICS
item.description:
Background: Dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEA-S) associates with disease severity in pulmonary hypertension (PH). However, prior studies focused on Group 1 disease; it is unknown whether DHEA-S associates with PH severity in other etiologies. It also remains unclear if DHEA-S associations with PH severity differ by sex or menopausal status.

Research question: Do associations between DHEA-S and measures of PH severity differ by PH etiology, sex, or menopausal status?

Study design and methods: We analyzed data from PVDOMICS, including 85 healthy controls and 710 participants with PH. Venous plasma DHEA-S levels were measured by ultraperformance liquid chromatography mass spectrometry. Multivariable regression models were used to examine associations between DHEA-S levels and invasive hemodynamics, right ventricular (RV) systolic function, and six-minute walk distance (6MWD). Analyses were stratified by sex and WSPH group, with exploratory stratification by menopausal status among subjects with Group 1 PH.

Results: DHEA-S levels were lower in all WSPH Groups compared with controls (adjusted p<0.01 for all). Associations between DHEA-S levels and PH severity metrics appeared most prominent in females with Group 1 PH. A doubling of DHEA-S was associated with a 2.8 mmHg (95% CI 1.6-4.1) lower mean pulmonary artery pressure, 3.2% (95% CI 2.0-4.4%) higher RV ejection fraction, and 22m (95% CI 11-33) farther 6MWD (all p<0.01). Higher DHEA-S associated with better RV function, but not pulmonary hemodynamics or 6MWD in females with Group 2 PH and males with Group 3 PH. In Group 1 PH, associations between DHEA-S and measures of PH severity appeared stronger in post-menopausal compared with premenopausal females.

Interpretation: Lower DHEA-S is a consistent feature across PH etiologies, but its association with disease severity appeared most pronounced in females with Group 1 PH. Modulation of DHEA-S levels or the pathways governing its regulation may represent a therapeutic target in PH, warranting further mechanistic study.

item.title: Lancet: Myocardial injury with non-obstructive coronary arteries: diagnostic pathways and stratified treatment
item.description:
Myocardial injury with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA), formerly known as myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries, challenges the long-standing assumption that myocardial infarction is synonymous with obstructive coronary artery disease. Rather than a paradox, MINOCA reflects the limitations of angiography-centred paradigms and the complexity of contemporary cardiovascular pathophysiology. Consistent with this updated definition, this Review approaches MINOCA as a working diagnosis that encompasses diverse mechanisms, including plaque disruption, coronary vasomotor dysfunction, microvascular disease, and non-coronary conditions. We propose a pragmatic, mechanism-oriented framework for selecting and sequencing complementary investigations, highlighting how intracoronary imaging, cardiac magnetic resonance, and coronary functional testing can be integrated according to the clinical scenario to refine diagnosis, while balancing diagnostic yield with procedural risk and resource availability. We discuss the implications for management, emphasising that treatment should be guided by underlying pathophysiology rather than a uniform approach derived from obstructive myocardial infarction. Emerging evidence supports the implementation of a stratified therapy to improve patient-centred outcomes. Finally, we discuss research priorities for improving mechanism-specific diagnosis and treatment, arguing that MINOCA represents both a conceptual advance and a transitional step toward a mechanism-based taxonomy of myocardial injury and infarction.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Decomposing time to hip fracture surgery into emergency department and post-emergency department delay
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Time to surgery after hip fracture is commonly reported as a single interval, but this does not show where delay occurs. For patients admitted through the emergency department (ED), total preoperative time includes ED and post-ED time.

Objective: To determine the relative contribution of ED and post-ED intervals to operative timing and whether prolonged ED length of stay (LOS) was associated with persistent downstream delay.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with hip fractures presenting to two EDs within one health system from January 2015 through October 2025. The pathway cohort required valid ED arrival, ED departure, and operative repair timestamps. The primary exposure was ED LOS greater than 8 h. The primary outcome was post-ED preoperative time.

Results: Of 605 candidate encounters, 426 had valid operative timing data. After excluding invalid pathway chronology and duplicate administrative rows linked to the same patient and operative timestamp, 381 patient operative episodes formed the deduplicated pathway cohort. Median ED LOS was 5.0 h, post-ED preoperative time was 19.9 h, and total preoperative time was 27.3 h. Prolonged ED LOS (23.1%) was associated with surgery after 24 and 36 h, but not longer post-ED preoperative time. Sensitivity analysis found an association after 48 h. Post-ED-only delay was more common than ED-only delay.

Conclusions: Prolonged ED LOS was associated with missed early surgery thresholds but did not explain most downstream delay. Separating ED and post-ED intervals may help hospitals distinguish ED throughput delay from later operative delay.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Emerging designer sedatives and adulterants in the emergency department: A narrative review
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: The illicit drug supply in the United States is rapidly evolving, with veterinary sedatives and novel synthetic opioids increasingly detected alongside fentanyl and other substances.

Objective: To review the epidemiology, clinical presentation, emergency department recognition and management, and public health implications of emerging veterinary sedatives and novel synthetic opioids in the illicit drug supply.

Discussion: Xylazine and medetomidine are α2-adrenergic agonists that may cause profound sedation, bradycardia, hypotension, and respiratory depression, particularly when combined with opioids. Naloxone remains indicated for suspected opioid co-exposure but does not reverse the effects of these non-opioid sedatives. Repeated xylazine exposure is associated with severe skin ulceration and soft-tissue injury, while medetomidine exposure may produce prolonged toxicity and a severe withdrawal syndrome characterized by hypertension, tachycardia, agitation, and autonomic instability. Nitazenes and orphine analogues are potent μ-opioid receptor agonists capable of causing severe and recurrent respiratory depression. Management centers on airway and ventilatory support and naloxone titrated to adequate ventilation, with repeated dosing or infusion when necessary. Recognition of these substances is complicated by polysubstance exposure and limited detection on routine hospital toxicology screens.

Conclusions: Emerging veterinary sedatives and novel synthetic opioids are creating increasingly complex overdose presentations in the emergency department. Persistent sedation after naloxone, unexplained bradycardia or hypotension, recurrent respiratory depression, severe autonomic withdrawal, and characteristic wounds should raise suspicion for emerging adulterants or synthetic opioids.

Introduction: Trauma-induced coagulopathy (TIC) causes significant morbidity and mortality in severely injured casualties. While low-titer group O whole blood (LTOWB) is increasingly used for prehospital resuscitation, the clinical value of active prehospital blood warming remains uncertain. We evaluated whether warmed LTOWB reduced TIC on emergency department (ED) arrival.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of combat casualties receiving prehospital LTOWB between October 27, 2023, and January 19, 2025 using linked data from the Israel Defense Forces Medical Corps Prehospital Trauma Registry and the Israeli National Trauma Registry. Patients were categorized by LTOWB administration method: active warming versus cold blood. The primary outcome was TIC on ED arrival (international normalized ratio ≥ 1.2). Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between warmed LTOWB and TIC, adjusting for prehospital shock, injury severity, severe head injury, transfusion volume, and acidosis on ED arrival.

Results: Of 275 casualties receiving prehospital LTOWB, 209 were included: 61 received warmed and 148 cold LTOWB. The median age was 23 years, and most patients sustained severe or critical injuries. TIC occurred in 54 patients (25.8%), including 13 (21.3%) receiving warmed and 41 (27.7%) receiving cold LTOWB. After adjustment, warmed LTOWB was not associated with lower odds of TIC (aOR 1.07; 95% CI, 0.45-2.49). Warming was also not associated with reduced massive transfusion or improved 24-h or 30-day survival.

Conclusion: Among combat casualties receiving prehospital LTOWB, active blood warming was not associated with reduced TIC on ED arrival. Larger studies are needed to clarify its clinical role.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Temporal course of seizure cluster resolution in children with benign convulsions with mild gastroenteritis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Benign convulsions with mild gastroenteritis (CwG) commonly present with clustered seizures, but their short-term temporal course remains incompletely quantified. We aimed to characterize seizure-cluster resolution and subsequent seizure occurrence over time to inform emergency department (ED) observation and disposition planning.

Methods: We retrospectively studied children younger than 6 years hospitalized with CwG between March 2016 and February 2026. Time to seizure cluster resolution (TSCR) was defined as the interval from first to final seizure onset. Kaplan-Meier analysis estimated cumulative cluster resolution. In the entire cohort, we also assessed subsequent seizures beyond selected times after the first seizure and after seizure-free intervals of 6, 12, and 18 h.

Results: Among 82 children, 50 (61.0%) had clustered seizures. Median TSCR was 6.1 h (IQR, 2.4-9.7). Cumulative cluster resolution was 50.0%, 84.0%, 90.0%, and 94.0% at 6, 12, 18, and 24 h, respectively. Subsequent seizures occurred beyond 6, 12, and 24 h after the first seizure in 30.5%, 9.8%, and 3.7% of children. After seizure-free intervals of at least 6 and 12 h, subsequent seizures occurred in 20.7% and 4.9%, respectively; none occurred after 18 h (95% CI, 0.0%-4.5%).

Conclusions: The seizure course of CwG was strongly front-loaded, with rapid cluster resolution and progressively fewer subsequent seizures as time elapsed and seizure-free intervals lengthened. These findings provide descriptive temporal benchmarks to inform ED observation and disposition planning.

Although glucocorticoids remain the cornerstone of therapy, treatment is frequently prolonged, associated with substantial toxic effects, and complicated by relapses. item.title: N Engl J Med: Blood-Pressure-Lowering Treatment across the Cardiovascular Risk Spectrum
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Treatment for lowering blood pressure reduces the risk of cardiovascular events among persons at high risk. Whether this benefit extends to those at lower risk remains unclear.

Methods: We performed a meta-analysis of individual participant data from randomized trials comparing antihypertensive treatment (intervention) with placebo, an active comparator, or usual care (comparator). The primary outcome was the first occurrence of a major cardiovascular event (fatal or nonfatal stroke, fatal or nonfatal ischemic heart disease, or heart failure resulting in death or hospitalization; composite outcome). Safety was assessed in trials that compared antihypertensive treatment with placebo or usual care, according to three prespecified composite outcomes: cardiovascular or hemodynamic events (palpitations, bradycardia, or hypotension), adverse renal events, and neurovestibular or fall-associated events. Participants were grouped into deciles according to predicted 5-year risk of a major cardiovascular event (median, 12.3%; lowest decile, <4%; highest decile, >27%).

Results: We included data from 51 trials and 357,440 participants - 169,042 in the intervention group and 188,398 in the comparator group. Over a median follow-up of 4.2 years, a major cardiovascular event occurred in 19,202 participants (11.4%) in the intervention group and in 24,398 (13.0%) in the comparator group. The overall estimated hazard ratio for a major cardiovascular event per 5-mm Hg reduction in systolic blood pressure was 0.90 (95% confidence interval, 0.88 to 0.92), with no evidence of variation across deciles. The absolute reduction in the 5-year cumulative risk of a major cardiovascular event was greater in the highest decile than in the lowest decile (2.6 vs. 0.4 percentage points), and the number needed to treat to prevent one major cardiovascular event over 5 years was lower in the highest decile than in the lowest decile (38 vs. 255). The incidence of a cardiovascular or hemodynamic event was 12.0 per 1000 person-years in the intervention group and 6.5 per 1000 person-years in the comparator group; the incidence of an adverse renal event was 3.3 and 2.2 per 1000 person-years, respectively; and the incidence of a neurovestibular or fall-associated event was 19.1 and 16.6 per 1000 person-years. The relative increase in the risk of each safety-outcome event with antihypertensive treatment as compared with placebo or usual care did not appear to vary across deciles.

Conclusions: Blood-pressure lowering was associated with a decreased risk of major cardiovascular events across the risk spectrum, including a predicted 5-year risk below 4%. (Funded by the British Heart Foundation; PROSPERO registry number, CRD42018099283.).

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Identification, Monitoring, and Management of Elevated Ketones in Ambulatory Settings: A Consensus Statement
item.description:
Importance: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), although preventable in most cases, is a leading cause of hospitalization in people with insulin-treated diabetes and is associated with suboptimal glycemic outcomes, increased risk for diabetes complications, and increased health care expenditure. This consensus statement outlines factors that may help identify individuals with diabetes who are at increased risk for elevated ketone levels; provides recommendations for ketone monitoring, including potential testing modalities; and discusses appropriate testing frequency and self-management strategies based on ketone severity.

Objective: To develop a clinical decision algorithm on the detection, monitoring, and management of elevated ketones in children, adolescents, and nonpregnant adults with diabetes.

Evidence review: For this consensus statement, 2 members of the American Diabetes Association Evidence Synthesis Team convened a panel of 13 external experts in diabetes, including clinicians, researchers, and certified diabetes care and education specialists, from May to October 2025. to systematically search PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, The Lens, and Semantic Scholar without date limits for literature on detecting ketones in people with diabetes. Relevant results were combined with citation searching and summarized; supplemental searches were also conducted for specific questions raised by the panel. The nominal group method was used for consensus and recommendations. Data were analyzed from October 2025 to January 2026.

Findings: Several factors may help identify people with diabetes who are at increased risk for elevated ketone levels, including those who require insulin therapy, who have a history of elevated hemoglobin A1c or episodes of DKA in the past year, or whose treatment regimen includes use of either an insulin pump or sodium glucose cotransporter inhibitor therapy. Situations that should prompt ketone monitoring, including prolonged hyperglycemia, dehydration, or nausea or vomiting, are reviewed along with ketone testing modalities, including capillary, urine, and emerging continuous ketone sensing technologies. A framework to allow people with diabetes to self-manage elevated ketones is presented, which grounds treatment based on ketone severity and specifies frequency of monitoring.

Conclusions and relevance: The algorithm presented in this consensus statement is meant to assist with early ketone detection and prevention of DKA. It is intended for health care professionals, policymakers, researchers, and developers of ketone monitoring tools to support current care while providing a foundation for future clinical applications as technologies evolve.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Simplified Regimen for Hypertension Management With Telemedicine and Blood Pressure Self-Monitoring: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Hypertension control remains difficult despite effective medications, motivating integrated remote-management strategies.

Objective: To test whether home blood pressure (BP) monitoring (HBPM), telemedicine, clinician-supervised titration, and single-pill combination (SPC) delivery improve office BP compared with usual care.

Design, setting, and participants: This open-label, multicenter randomized clinical trial enrolled adults aged 18 to 75 years with treated essential hypertension who met protocol-defined office BP thresholds at screening at 4 Chinese medical centers from January 1, 2021, through July 20, 2023. Participants were randomized 1:1. Data were analyzed from December 18, 2025, through February 10, 2026, based on modified intention to treat.

Interventions: All participants received a free HBPM device and a 2-week equivalent SPC run-in. After randomization, both groups continued HBPM; the intervention group also received telemedicine review, clinician-supervised titration, and free medication and delivery.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the between-group difference in change in office systolic BP (SBP) from baseline, assessed after the run-in and at randomization, to 6 months, analyzed using an independent-samples t test. Secondary outcomes included office diastolic BP (DBP), rate of BP control, and adverse events.

Results: Among 364 participants (mean [SD] age, 54 [11] years; 195 male [53.6%]), 180 were randomized to the intervention group and 184 to usual care. A total of 163 intervention participants and 172 usual care participants had baseline and 6-month SBP data. Office SBP decreased by a mean (SD) of 9.7 (16.5) mm Hg in the intervention group and 5.8 (16.8) mm Hg in usual care (between-group difference, -3.9 [95% CI, -7.5 to -0.3] mm Hg; P = .03). Office DBP decreased by a mean (SD) of 4.2 (11.1) vs 1.1 (11.8) mm Hg (difference, -3.1 [95% CI, -5.6 to -0.7] mm Hg; P = .02). Office BP was controlled in 132 of 180 participants (73.3%) for the intervention vs 124 of 184 (67.4%) for usual care (P = .27). Adverse events occurred in 24 of 180 intervention participants (13.3%) vs 15 of 184 usual care participants (8.2%) (P = .13), and adverse event-related treatment discontinuation occurred in 15 (8.3%) vs 1 (0.5%), respectively (P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial of adults with treated essential hypertension and elevated office BP at screening, the integrated intervention produced a modestly greater reduction in office BP than usual care at 6 months. Longer-term and implementation studies are needed to evaluate the closed-loop remote management pathway.

Trial registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry Identifier: ChiCTR2000037217.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Food Insecurity During Pregnancy and Child Neurodevelopmental Outcomes
item.description:
Importance: Food insecurity affects over 12% of adults in the US and has been associated with adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes. However, little is known about the relationship between food insecurity during pregnancy and child neurodevelopmental outcomes.

Objective: To determine whether food insecurity during pregnancy is associated with greater risk of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) including autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study included pregnant individuals in the Kaiser Permanente Northern California integrated health system surveyed between June 2020 and September 2022 and their children followed up through December 2025.

Exposures: Food insecurity measured using the Hunger as a Vital Sign Questionnaire.

Main outcomes and measures: NDD and ASD diagnoses were determined by the presence of International Classification of Diseases, Ninth Revision (ICD-9) and International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes in child electronic health records. Adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) for any NDD and ASD diagnoses were estimated separately using Cox models adjusted for maternal age, neighborhood deprivation index, insurance type, parity, prepregnancy body mass index, prepregnancy depression, child birth year, and sex. Participation in food assistance programs was evaluated as a modifier of the association between food insecurity and NDD risk.

Results: Of a total 21 376 pregnant individuals who responded, 13 285 met criteria for inclusion in analysis (mean [SD] age at delivery, 32.7 [4.5] years; 2781 Asian [20.9%], 410 Black [3.1%], 2628 Hispanic [19.8%], 6505 White [49.0%]); 1599 (12.0%) reported food insecurity. Of the children in the cohort (6835 male [51.4%]), 2741 (20.6%) were diagnosed with NDD and 690 (5.2%) with ASD. Food insecurity during pregnancy was associated with greater risk of both any NDD (aHR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.10-1.38) and ASD (aHR, 1.49; 95% CI, 1.21-1.80). Risk was elevated only among those who did not receive food assistance both for NDD (no food assistance: aHR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.11-1.43; food assistance: aHR, 1.04; 95% CI, 0.80-1.34) and ASD (no food assistance: aHR, 1.69; 95% CI, 1.36-2.10; food assistance: aHR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.49-1.22).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of mother-child pairs in a Northern California health system, food insecurity during pregnancy was associated with greater risk of NDDs. Participation in food assistance programs by households that experience food insecurity may provide health benefits for children; children born to households experiencing food insecurity may benefit from earlier developmental screening and monitoring.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Clinical Cutoff Scores for the Problematic Media Use Measure in the ABCD Study
item.description:
Importance: Dysregulated digital media use that interferes with functioning, or problematic media use (PMU), is a growing concern for child development. Although measures can capture PMU as a dimensional construct, scales lack risk cutoffs for early adolescents (aged 11-15 years).

Objective: To establish cutoff scores for the Problematic Media Use Measure (PMUM) and examine criterion validity.

Design, setting, and participants: This longitudinal cohort study with a 4-year follow-up analyzed data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, release 6.0. The cohort represented ABCD Study adolescents with follow-up data for waves 2 through 5; the longitudinal sample included adolescents with PMUM data at all 4 waves.

Exposures: Problematic media use as measured by developed PMUM cutoff scores.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes included parent-reported internalizing and externalizing symptoms, measured using the Child Behavior Checklist, and academic performance, measured by parent-reported grades over the past year. Four time points were analyzed in July 2026: time 1, 2019 to 2020 (age 11-12 years); time 2, 2020 to 2021 (age 12-13 years); time 3, 2021 to 2022 (age 13-14 years); and time 4, 2022 to 2023 (age 14-15 years). Item response theory was used to establish cutoff scores. Longitudinal models were used to examine criterion validity.

Results: At time 1, the cohort included 10 435 adolescents aged 11 to 12 years (5465 male [52.4%]). Cross-sectional samples were 9749, 9033, and 8262 participants at times 2, 3, and 4, respectively. A total of 6623 completed all 4 time points. Cutoff scores for PMUM were 9 to 22 for the not-at-risk level, 23 to 34 for the at-risk level, and 35 to 45 for the high-risk level. Applying the PMUM cutoff scores cross-sectionally, high-risk prevalence was stable across waves (time 1, 642 participants [6.2%]; time 2, 649 participants [6.7%]; time 3, 592 participants [6.6%]; time 4, 543 participants [6.6%]), and at-risk prevalence declined (time 1, 3677 participants [35.2%]; time 2, 3238 participants [33.2%]; time 3, 2902 participants [32.1%]; time 4, 2554 participants [30.9%]). Risk groups differed on outcomes at every wave. Averaged across the 4 waves, median (IQR) internalizing symptom T scores were 45 (38-52) for the not-at-risk group, 51 (44-58) for the at-risk group, and 57 (48-65) for the high-risk group; median (IQR) externalizing symptom T scores were 40 (34-46), 46 (40-54), and 55 (46-62), respectively; and median (IQR) grades were 4 (3-4), 4 (3-4), and 3 (2-4), respectively (all P < .001). In the criterion lagged model adjusting for the prior outcome and sex, the at-risk classification estimated next-wave internalizing symptoms (b = 0.12 [95% CI, 0.10-0.15]), externalizing symptoms (b = 0.13 [95% CI, 0.11-0.15]), and grades (b = -0.08 [95% CI, -0.10 to -0.05]) (all P < .001), and high risk classification showed more pronounced associations (internalizing symptoms: b = 0.22 [95% CI, 0.18-0.27]; externalizing symptoms: b = 0.22 [0.18-0.27]; grades: b = -0.19 [95% CI, -0.24 to -0.15] (all P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: This cohort study of adolescents showed that PMUM cutoff scores were prospectively associated with behavioral, emotional, and academic outcomes across 4 annual waves of the ABCD Study. These thresholds may be useful for identifying adolescents at greatest need for intervention.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Maternal Prepregnancy Body Mass Index and Developmental Vulnerability at 36 Months
item.description:
Importance: Maternal prepregnancy body mass index (BMI) is increasingly relevant in Asia, but its association with domain-specific developmental vulnerability in early childhood remains unclear.

Objective: To investigate the associations of maternal prepregnancy BMI with multidomain and domain-specific developmental vulnerability (DV) at age 3 years.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective, nationally representative cohort study used 6-month and 36-month follow-up data from the 2005 Taiwan Birth Cohort. Data analysis was performed from February to June 2026. Of 21 248 mother-child pairs at baseline, 18 577 complete-case pairs were analyzed at 36 months after excluding multiple births, participants lost to follow-up, and those with missing covariate or milestone data.

Exposures: Self-reported maternal prepregnancy BMI was categorized by Taiwan Health Promotion Administration criteria as underweight (<18.5), normal weight (18.5-23.9), overweight (24.0-26.9), and obesity (≥27.0). Covariates, including maternal sociodemographic characteristics, pregnancy and perinatal outcomes, and paternal BMI, were selected using a directed acyclic graph.

Main outcomes and measures: Child DV was defined as milestone nonattainment beyond cohort-specific empirical thresholds (greater than 90th percentile) at 36 months, based on caregiver-reported sentinel milestones collected during structured home visits. DV is a population-level screening indicator, not a clinical diagnosis of developmental delay. Multidomain DV (MDV) was defined as DV in greater than or equal to 2 of 5 domains.

Results: Among the 18 577 mother-child pairs analyzed (maternal mean [SD] age, 28.85 [4.83] years; female infants, 8849 [47.6%]; mean [SD] gestational age, 38.38 [1.52] weeks; maternal underweight, 3725 [20.1%]; normal weight, 12 180 [65.6%]; overweight, 1659 [8.9%]; obesity, 1013 [5.4%]), MDV showed a U-shaped pattern across maternal BMI categories. Compared with normal weight, maternal underweight was associated with a higher risk of MDV (adjusted risk ratio [aRR], 1.19; 95% CI, 1.06-1.33). Maternal obesity was associated more clearly with language-domain vulnerability (aRR, 1.56; 95% CI, 1.25-1.94) than with MDV after adjustment (aRR, 1.22; 95% CI, 0.97-1.54). Mediation analyses suggested limited mediation by recorded gestational complications.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 18 577 mother-child pairs in Taiwan, maternal underweight was associated with a higher risk of MDV at 36 months, while maternal obesity was associated more clearly with language-domain vulnerability than with overall MDV. These findings suggested that preconception weight optimization and developmental surveillance warranted consideration of both extremes of maternal BMI.
