item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Neonatal Care Length of Stay and Physiological Readiness for Discharge in Preterm Newborns
item.description:
Importance: Preterm neonates need long hospital stays. Unnecessarily prolonged hospitalization can worsen outcomes, exacerbate parental stress, and increase costs of care.

Objective: To identify the postmenstrual age (PMA) when preterm neonates reach physiological maturity for discharge (breathing without support, feeding orally, and weighing ≥1700 g), the PMA at discharge from neonatal care, and the number of care days between physiological readiness and discharge.

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter, population-based cohort study used the UK National Neonatal Research Database and included all neonatal units in England and Wales (data from January 1, 2016, to December 31, 2023, were analyzed between June 2024 and June 2025). Participants were hospitalized preterm neonates (<37 weeks' gestational age [GA]) without a lethal congenital anomaly who were admitted for at least 48 hours and survived to discharge home.

Main outcomes and measures: PMA at physiological readiness for discharge and at discharge and the number of days of difference between the 2.

Results: There were 238 563 neonates (129 671 [54.4%] males), with median GA of 34 weeks (IQR, 32-35 weeks) and birth weight of 2090 g (IQR, 1635-2508 g). Overall, 19.5% (60.7% of those born at 22-24 weeks' GA) were discharged before reaching physiological readiness. Among the remaining neonates, the median PMA at physiological readiness was 36 (IQR, 35-36) weeks. This was later in more premature neonates (40 [IQR, 38-42] weeks in those born at 22-24 weeks' GA vs 35 [IQR, 35-36] weeks in those born at >31 weeks' GA). Overall, neonates stayed in the hospital for a median of 2 (IQR, 1-4) days after reaching physiological readiness. This difference was longer in more premature neonates: 4 (IQR, 1-7) days in those born at 22 to 24 weeks' GA, 4 (IQR, 2-7) days in those born at 25 to 27 weeks, 3 (IQR, 2-6) days in those born at 28 to 31 weeks, and 2 (IQR, 1-4) days in those born at more than 32 weeks. Overall, median (IQR) length of stay decreased with increasing birth GA: for neonates born at 22 to 24 weeks' GA, it was 125 (IQR, 109-144) days; at 25 to 29 weeks, 89 (IQR, 75-106) days; at 28 to 31 weeks, 45 (IQR, 35-59) days; at 32 to 33 weeks, 21 (IQR, 16-27) days; and at 34 to 36 weeks, 8 (IQR, 4-13) days.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, neonates born more preterm achieved physiological readiness for discharge at higher PMAs and had longer periods in the hospital after reaching physiological readiness. The findings suggest that research and services should focus on clinical measures of discharge readiness and incorporate parental and social factors and inequity to optimize length of stay without unintended adverse impact on family stress.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Polygenic Risk Scores and PSA Levels for Risk of Prostate Cancer and Related Mortality
item.description:
Importance: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing is the standard method for prostate screening and long-term risk assessment. Given the high heritability for prostate cancer (PCa), genetic factors may provide additional value.

Objective: To inform risk-stratified PCa screening strategies beyond PSA alone by integrating genetic risk.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study included individuals from the Stockholm3 (STHLM3) study, a prospective, population-based screening trial that enrolled men aged 50 to 69 years in Stockholm, Sweden, between May 2012 and December 2014. Of 59 088 eligible men without prior PCa who consented, 59 067 with a valid PSA test were included. PCa outcomes were recorded from inclusion until December 31, 2023. Data were analyzed from April 2025 to January 2026.

Exposures: Men were categorized by baseline PSA level and genetic risk; first-degree family history of PCa was assessed for all, while a 232-variant polygenic risk score (PRS) was calculated for those with PSA levels of 1 ng/mL or greater, per trial design.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcomes were clinically significant disease (defined as International Society of Urological Pathology grade ≥2) and PCa-specific mortality. Cause-specific hazard ratios (HR) and 2-, 6-, and 10-year absolute risks were stratified by PSA level at entry and genetic risk and estimated using regression standardization.

Results: Among the 59 067 individuals included in the analysis, the median age at inclusion was 60.6 (IQR, 55.1-65.7) years. The 10-year risk of clinically significant disease was 0.5% among men with PSA level less than 1 ng/mL and doubled with a positive family history (HR, 2.38 [95% CI, 1.57-3.59]). For PSA levels of 1 to 3 ng/mL, the 10-year risk was 5.9%, tripling in the PRS category of greater than 80% to 100% compared with PRS category of 0 to 20% (HR, 3.53 [95% CI, 2.36-5.28]). For PSA levels of 3 ng/mL or greater, the 10-year risk was 21%, with a similar PRS association (HR, 2.31 [95% CI, 1.86-2.86]). PRS category of greater than 80% to 100% was associated with higher PCa-specific mortality (HR, 2.71 [95% CI, 1.19-6.16]). Based on absolute risks, several genetic groups exceeded established thresholds for further investigation.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 59 067 men from the STHLM3 study, a PRS and family history provided meaningful 10-year risk stratification for clinically significant disease and PCa-specific death for men with PSA levels of 1 ng/mL or greater, suggesting that genetic information may contribute to risk refinement within PSA-based screening for PCa.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Clinical Features and Outcomes of Adenovirus Infections in Critically Ill Patients: A Retrospective Multicenter Case-Matched Analysis
item.description:
Objectives: Human adenovirus (HAdV) infection can lead to severe organ involvement in the ICU, particularly among immunocompromised patients. In this study of ICU patients with HAdV infection, we aimed to 1) determine the prevalence of HAdV disease, 2) identify risk factors for HAdV disease, and 3) evaluate its association with ICU mortality.

Design: Retrospective, multicenter, and propensity score case-matched study.

Setting: Eight ICUs in France.

Patients: Adult ICU patients admitted between January 2011 and January 2024 with at least one positive HAdV polymerase chain reaction result from any biological sample were included. HAdV infections were classified as either localized infections or systemic HAdV disease.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: A total of 169 patients were analyzed, including 115 patients (68%) classified as localized HAdV infection and 54 patients (32%) as HAdV disease. Hematologic malignancies were significantly more frequent in patients with HAdV disease (74% vs. 37%; p < 0.001). Twenty-three patients (43%) with HAdV disease received allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Pneumonia was the main end-organ manifestation (n = 36/54; 67%). By multivariate analysis, allogeneic HSCT (odds ratio [OR], 3.04) and corticosteroid therapy (OR, 2.89) were independently associated with HAdV disease. ICU mortality was 45% (n = 76). By multivariate analysis, HAdV disease (OR, 3.15), performance status greater than or equal to 2 (OR, 3.35), and Sequential Organ Failure Assessment scores at admission (OR, 1.17 per point) were independently associated with ICU mortality. Mortality remained significantly higher in the HAdV disease group (OR, 10.50) compared with matched ICU patients without HAdV infection.

Conclusions: HAdV disease occurred in approximately one-third of ICU patients with HAdV infection, predominantly among those with hematologic malignancies or corticosteroid therapy, and was independently associated with mortality.

item.title: JAMA: Telehealth to Support Coordinated Spontaneous Awakening and Breathing Trials in Invasive Ventilation: The TEACH Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Coordinated spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials (C-SAT/SBT) improve outcomes for patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation, but implementation remains inadequate.

Objective: To evaluate whether a telehealth intervention added to a standard audit and feedback implementation of C-SAT/SBT increases adherence and improves outcomes compared with standard audit and feedback implementation alone (control).

Design, setting, and participants: A cluster randomized type 2 hybrid effectiveness-implementation clinical trial was conducted in 12 Intermountain Health hospitals in Utah and Idaho. Patients aged 16 years or older who were intubated and mechanically ventilated in the intensive care unit were enrolled from December 1, 2022, until July 31, 2025, with last follow-up on January 23, 2026.

Intervention: Telehealth hospitals received real-time oversight from telecritical care nurses and respiratory therapists for adherence to C-SAT/SBT and a standard audit and feedback implementation. Control hospitals received only standard audit and feedback.

Main outcomes and measures: Co-primary outcome measures were adherence to C-SAT/SBT and ventilator-free days to day 28. C-SAT/SBT was defined as any day that the SAT and SBT were separately adherent, and the SAT followed the SBT within 2 hours or both occurred before noon, or the patient was extubated. Change in adherence from baseline was compared between groups using a mixed-effects logistic model with prespecified 1-sided significance testing. Change in ventilator-free days was compared using a mixed-effects proportional odds model.

Results: There were 4544 patients at telehealth hospitals, 6438 patients at control hospitals, and 1789 preimplementation common baseline patients (median [IQR] age, 62 [47-71] years; 4826 [37.8%] female). The baseline C-SAT/SBT adherence rate of 43.9% increased to 90.3% at telehealth intervention hospitals and to 77.6% at control hospitals (odds ratio for change in telehealth vs change in control, 2.87; 1-sided 95% lower confidence limit, 2.44; P < .001; absolute difference, 11.4%; 95% CI, 8.8%-14.3%). Median (IQR) ventilator-free days from a common baseline of 24 (0-26) increased to 25 (10-27) at telehealth intervention hospitals and 25 (1-27) at control hospitals (odds ratio for change in telehealth vs change in control, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.01-1.45, P = .04; absolute difference, 1.02 days; 95% CI, 0.05-1.96 days).

Conclusions and relevance: Among adults intubated and mechanically ventilated in the intensive care unit, adding real-time telehealth support for C-SAT/SBT improved adherence and increased ventilator-free days more than a standard audit and feedback implementation alone.

item.title: J Addict Med: DSM-5 Substance Use Disorder Severity, Treatment, and Self-identified Recovery Among US Parents
item.description:
Objectives: More information is needed about the national landscape regarding DSM-5 substance use disorder (SUD) severity, treatment, and recovery among US parents residing with their children. This study examines how many US parents living with their children have a past-year DSM-5 SUD, how many have received substance use treatment, and the number of parents in abstinent versus nonabstinent self-identified recovery.

Methods: Nationally representative data from the 2023 National Survey on Drug Use and Health among the US civilian, noninstitutionalized population (≥12 y) were used. Weighted counts, percentages, and 95% CIs of past-year DSM-5 SUD involving alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, hallucinogens, heroin, inhalants, methamphetamine, nonmedical prescription benzodiazepines, opioids, or stimulants were estimated, including SUD severity, treatment, perceived problem, and self-identified recovery.

Results: An estimated 10,440,020 US parents living with their children experienced past-year DSM-5 SUD, including 4,318,360 with moderate-or-severe SUD. Among parents with a past-year SUD, many did not perceive a substance use problem, and only 16.0% received past-year SUD treatment. More than 7 in 10 parents with a past-year SUD had not received treatment nor were in recovery. Of 5,288,968 parents in self-identified recovery, 31.5% were abstinent, and 68.5% were nonabstinent.

Conclusions: Over 10 million US parents residing with their children have a past-year DSM-5 SUD, 84% of whom did not receive SUD treatment. There is a wide SUD treatment gap among US parents, and a lack of problem recognition appears to be a major driver. Screening and early detection of SUD, along with access to evidence-based treatment, are needed.

item.title: Crit Care: The MIME framework for non-invasive longitudinal assessment of inspiratory effort during pressure support ventilation: a physiological validation study
item.description:
Background: Continuous monitoring of inspiratory effort during assisted mechanical ventilation remains challenging, yet it is vital as the transition from controlled to assisted mechanical ventilation requires careful titration of inspiratory effort to ensure patient safety. The Mixed Integer Multi-Effort (MIME) method is a physiological modeling approach that uses standard ventilator signals to non-invasively estimate inspiratory muscle pressure (Pmus). We evaluated the accuracy of MIME during pressure support ventilation (PSV) in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF).

Methods: We conducted a prospective physiological validation study in adult patients with AHRF within 48 h of their first transition from controlled mechanical ventilation to PSV. Airway and esophageal pressure, flow, and volume, were recorded and analyzed offline with the MIME algorithm, which estimates Pmus by reconstructing airway pressure and separating ventilator-delivered from patient-generated pressure using a respiratory mechanics-based model. MIME-derived Pmus estimates were compared with esophageal pressure-derived Pmus using Bland-Altman analysis with mixed-effects modeling to account for repeated measurements within patients. Receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to evaluate MIME's ability to detect high and low inspiratory effort and to compare its performance with end-expiratory occlusion pressure (ΔPocc).

Results: Sixty-two independent model-fitting windows (1240 breaths) from 18 patients were analyzed. Median inspiratory Pmus was 7.5 (IQR 6.0-9.1) cmH₂O for MIME-derived estimates and 6.9 (5.9-8.9) cmH₂O for esophageal pressure-derived measurements. Breath-by-breath analysis demonstrated a mean difference of 0.4 cmH₂O with limits of agreement ranging from - 3.4 to 4.2 cmH₂O. Agreement between methods improved when inspiratory effort was averaged over multiple breaths. Averaged values within each analyzed recording set showed a mean difference of 0.4 cmH₂O with limits of agreement ranging from - 2.2 to 3.0 cmH₂O. MIME demonstrated good discriminative performance in detecting both high and low inspiratory effort (AUROC 0.83 and 0.88, respectively). Compared with ΔPocc, MIME showed similar performance for detecting low inspiratory effort, whereas ΔPocc performed better for detecting high inspiratory effort.

Conclusions: The MIME method provided non-invasive estimates of inspiratory effort during pressure support ventilation and may complement established physiological tools such as ΔPocc by supporting longitudinal assessment. Validation in broader populations and physiological settings, together with dedicated assessment of convergence and computational performance, is required before real-time bedside implementation.

item.title: Crit Care: Effect of positive end-expiratory pressure on intracranial pressure, cerebral perfusion pressure and brain-tissue oxygenation in acute brain injury: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
item.description:
Background: The effect of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) on the injured brain is uncertain, and existing evidence is usually reduced to a single high-versus-low contrast. We quantified the dose-response relationship between PEEP and intracranial pressure (ICP), cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) and brain-tissue oxygenation (PbtO₂) in adults with acute brain injury (ABI).

Methods: We systematically searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL and Web of Science to 5 July 2026 (PRISMA 2020). Within-patient PEEP-titration studies formed a primary layer; between-patient and observational studies formed a separate secondary layer. Overlapping cohorts were resolved by a pre-specified anti-duplication rule. Study-clustered multilevel meta-regression with cluster-robust (CR2) variance estimated the slope of each outcome per cmH₂O of PEEP; restricted cubic splines tested non-linearity. Robustness was examined with a one-stage dose-response model reconstructing the within-study covariance, prediction intervals, leave-one-out, leave-cluster-out analyses, publication-bias tests and pre-specified effect modifiers. Certainty was rated with GRADE against pre-anchored minimal important differences (MID; ICP 2 mmHg, CPP 5 mmHg).

Results: Of 4471 records, 37 studies were included. In the primary layer (410 patients), ICP rose + 0.118 mmHg per cmH₂O (95% CI 0.046 to 0.189; p = 0.006; 12 studies, 31 contrasts) - +0.59 mmHg per 5 cmH₂O, entirely below the 2 mmHg MID - with no departure from linearity across the sampled range of 3-21 cmH₂O (non-linearity p = 0.82), corroborated by the one-stage model (+ 0.133; 0.065 to 0.202). Evidence above 15 cmH₂O was confined to two contrasts from one study; restricted to ≤ 15 cmH₂O the slope was + 0.134 (0.071 to 0.197). CPP fell - 0.177 mmHg per cmH₂O (- 0.339 to - 0.015; p = 0.038; 10 studies, 379 patients), less than one fifth of the 5 mmHg MID; the estimate was of similar magnitude (- 0.168) when ICP, MAP and CPP were modelled in an identical set of contrasts. In that common set the ICP component was estimated with precision and the arterial component was not. Effect modifiers derived from individual studies suggested larger effects with non-recruitable lungs, lung injury/obesity and low intracranial compliance; prediction intervals crossed zero. Small-study asymmetry was not detectable. Certainty was low for ICP and low for CPP; PbtO₂ was not estimable.

Conclusions: Across the available within-patient evidence, raising PEEP is associated with a small, linear increase in ICP that is, on average, well below accepted minimal important differences over the PEEP range studied, with a correspondingly small change in CPP. The convergence of exploratory modifier analyses generates the hypothesis that the effect is concentrated in patients with non-recruitable lungs, a stiff chest wall or reduced intracranial compliance, in whom PEEP should be titrated under multimodal neuromonitoring. This hypothesis requires prospective, phenotype-stratified testing.

Registration: PROSPERO CRD420261442522 (registered 5 July 2026).

item.title: Chest: Impact of Steroid-sparing Immunosuppressants on Lung Function and Mortality in Fibrotic Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
item.description:
Background: Evidence supporting steroid-sparing immunosuppressants (SSIs) in fibrotic hypersensitivity pneumonitis (f-HP) remains limited.

Review question: Do SSIs improve lung function or survival in adults with f-HP?

Study design and methods: Following Cochrane and PRISMA 2020 guidance (PROSPERO CRD420261413825), we searched MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar through May 2026 for studies of mycophenolate, azathioprine, methotrexate, leflunomide, tacrolimus, or cyclophosphamide. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and appraised studies using ROBINS-I, JBI, or Newcastle-Ottawa tools. DerSimonian-Laird random-effects models pooled percent-predicted FVC and DLCO changes and hazard ratios for death or lung transplantation. GRADE assessed certainty.

Results: Seventeen studies (1,341 patients) were included. SSIs were associated with modest FVC stabilization (13 studies; +1.11% predicted, 95% CI 0.37-1.84; I2=0%) and DLCO stabilization (9 studies; +3.73% predicted, 95% CI 2.56-4.90; I2=24%). The estimand-consistent mortality pool of two adjusted overall-effect studies demonstrated no survival benefit and could not exclude harm (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.86-2.26; I2=0%). Certainty was low for lung function and very low for mortality. Descriptive benefit was concentrated in patients with identifiable antigens and less radiologic fibrosis.

Interpretation: Modest lung-function stabilization largely reflects uncontrolled within-group changes, not definitive disease modification. Controlled survival evidence remains insufficient; adequately powered randomized trials are needed.

item.title: Lancet: Sexual wellbeing in Britain: findings from the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4)
item.description:
Background: Sexual wellbeing is an individual state of feeling respected, safe, and comfortable with sex and sexuality, and having self-esteem, agency, and support in one's sexual life. It is related to, but distinct from, sexual function and sexual health. The epidemiology of sexual wellbeing in a general population is not well understood. We aimed to examine inequalities in low sexual wellbeing, and discover associations with sexual behaviour, sexual and reproductive health experiences, and general and mental health. We sought to understand which individual items within our validated 13-item measure of sexual wellbeing (the Natsal-SW) are most strongly associated with key sexual health behaviours and indicators.

Methods: We conducted the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4), which is a large nationally representative cross-sectional study of people aged 16-59 years who are resident in Britain (data used here collected between Sept 20, 2022, and Dec 3, 2023). 4160 participants reporting sexual experience ever completed the Natsal-SW; standardised score range 0-52, low selected as ≤33, and high as ≥48. Focusing attention on those with most need, we used age-adjusted logistic regressions to examine associations with low sexual wellbeing.

Findings: The weighted prevalence of current low sexual wellbeing was similar in women (14·3% [95% CI 12·6-16·3]) and men (13·7% [11·7-15·9]), but high sexual wellbeing was slightly less prevalent in women than men (20·7% [95% CI 18·7- 22·8] vs 24·4% [21·8- 27·1]; p=0·024). Nine items on Natsal-SW differed by gender; notably women were more likely to report feeling upset with others about past sexual events, and men to report feeling ashamed about sexual thoughts. The odds of low sexual wellbeing were greater among young people (aged 16-24 years), individuals from sexual and gender minorities, individuals reporting lower income and, among women only, educational level. Low sexual wellbeing was associated with reporting first sex after age 25 years, symptoms of sexually-transmitted infections and less frequent sex in the past month, at least four partners, distressing sexual problems, and sexual violence in the past year, and at least one same-sex partner in the past 5 years. Low sexual wellbeing was associated with currently screening positive for depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-2-item) and anxiety (Generalised Anxiety Disorder-2-item) symptoms and low mental wellbeing, particularly among men. Associations between key sexual health and behaviour indicators, and low sexual wellbeing, remained after adjustment for mental health.

Interpretation: Low sexual wellbeing is unequally distributed, and patterns of association differ notably from sexual health. These data support future inclusion of sexual wellbeing in population health policy and intervention.

item.title: Lancet: Prevalence and trends in sexual behaviour in Britain from 1990 to 2024: findings from the repeated cross-sectional National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal)
item.description:
Background: Contemporary data on sexual behaviour are needed to inform and evaluate sexual and reproductive health strategies and services and understand societal shifts. In this assessment of the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), we aimed to provide up-to-date prevalence estimates and examine changes in key sexual behaviours in Britain reported between 1990 and 2024.

Methods: The Natsal study is repeat cross-sectional probability-sample surveys of the British population, undertaken approximately decennially since 1990. Natsal-4 (2022-24) used interviewer-administered and self-completion questionnaires, among two probability samples: an address-based sample and a probability panel. Data were weighted to broadly align with Britain's sociodemographic structure. In Natsal-4, prevalence of sexual experiences, partner numbers, frequency of sex, and online behaviours are presented by age and gender among participants aged 16-59 years, with changes in prevalence across Natsal surveys presented by age and gender among participants aged 16-44 years.

Findings: Of 6719 Natsal-4 participants (aged 16-59 years), 89·4% (95% CI 88·3-90·4) reported ever having sex (median five lifetime partners for both women and men). In the past year, 77·0% (95% CI 75·6-78·4) reported having had sex, and 65·5% (63·9-67·0) reported one sexual partner. Reporting at least one new partner in the past year was highest among participants aged 16-24 years (21·7% [95% CI 17·3-26·8] in women, 30·1% [24·5-36·4] in men). Pornography use and sexting (sending or receiving sexual images) in the past year were more common among men (80·7% [95% CI 78·6-82·6] and 26·0% [23·9-28·3], respectively) than among women (36·6% [34·7-38·5] and 22·2% [20·5-23·9], respectively); both were higher among younger age groups. The proportion of 16-24-year-olds who reported never having had sex increased from 18·9% (95% CI 17·0-20·9) in Natsal-3 (2010-12) to 37·7% (36·2-43·1) in Natsal-4 (2022-24) among women; and 18·2% (16·2-20·4) to 28·4% (23·1-34·5) among men. Reporting of same-sex sex increased among 16-44-year-olds from 6·8% (95% CI 6·1-7·6) in 2010-12 to 14·0% (12·4-15·7) in 2022-24 among women, and from 4·0% (3·3-4·7) to 12·3% (10·4-14·5) among men. Among 16-44-year-olds, we found a decline in average frequency of sex from four times per month in Natsal-1 (1990) to twice per month in Natsal-4 (2022-24).

Interpretation: Sexual behaviour in Britain has shifted markedly since 1990, including a recent decline in sexual experience among young people and increased reporting of same-sex attraction and behaviour across all age groups. Sexual and reproductive health policies and services remain essential and must adapt to shifting needs and new areas of risk and vulnerability, including safe engagement in online sexual activity.

item.title: Lancet: Sexually transmitted infections, behavioural risks, and uptake of sexual health services in Britain from 2010 to 2024: findings from the repeated cross-sectional National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal)
item.description:
Background: Sexually transmitted infection (STI) diagnoses have increased in Britain since 2010, alongside major changes to sexual health policy, services, and disruptions owing to the COVID-19 pandemic. Meanwhile, sexual activity has decreased at population level, and more people report same-sex behaviours. To understand implications for HIV and STI control, we examined the general population prevalence of three STIs, sexual behaviours associated with STIs, and uptake of sexual health services, including HIV and chlamydia testing.

Methods: We conducted the fourth National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4) between Sept 20, 2022, and April 5, 2024. In this analysis, we used cross-sectional data from 5949 sexually experienced (who reported ever having sex) participants aged 16-59 years in Britain from the probability sample surveys. We estimated weighted prevalences for STIs using biosamples (vaginal swabs or urine samples; n=2721), self-reported STI-associated behaviours (including a composite of ≥4 partners, condomless sex with ≥2 partners in the past year, or overlapping partners in the past 5 years), and sexual health service uptake. Comparisons were made between groups defined by partners' sex and over time by comparing with Natsal-3 (2010-12).

Findings: In Natsal-4, overall prevalence of Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, and Trichomonas vaginalis was less than 1·0%. C trachomatis prevalence was highest in women aged 16-24 years (4·0%, 95% CI 1·3-11·7). STI-associated behaviours (composite) were most prevalent in young people (aged 16-24 years) with only opposite-sex partners (women 26·5%, 95% CI 20·2-33·9; men 29·4%, 22·5-37·6), women reporting sex with women and men (WSWM; 60·0%, 49·0-70·1), and men reporting sex with men (MSM; 57·1%, 48·6-65·3). Among those with only opposite-sex partners, past-year uptake was higher in women than men for sexual health service use (women 8·3%, 7·2-9·6; men 3·9%, 3·0-5·1), HIV testing (women 5·8%, 4·9-7·0; men 2·8%, 2·1-3·7), and chlamydia testing (women 8·4%, 7·1-10·1; men 4·7%, 3·4-6·4). Among participants reporting STI-associated behaviours, apart from MSM (47·3%, 36·1-58·8), the majority of people who reported STI-associated behaviours had not taken up services (eg, for sexual health services in participants with opposite-sex partners: women 73·8%, 67·8-79·1; men 84·9%, 79·4-89·4; WSWM 68·6%, 54.1-80.2). Between Natsal-3 and Natsal-4, HIV testing increased in MSM, sexual health service use decreased in young men with only opposite-sex partners, and chlamydia testing markedly declined (eg, in all women aged 16-24 years: Natsal-3 54·2%, 51·4-57·0; Natsal-4 17·8%, 12·7-24·5).

Interpretation: Many people remain at behavioural risk for STIs, particularly young people, WSWM, and MSM. Most people with STI-associated behaviours had not used sexual health services in the past year. Declining chlamydia testing and high prevalence in young women might cause reproductive harm. Universal sexual health services remain essential.

item.title: Lancet: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, vaccination, and cervical screening in Britain from 1999 to 2024: findings from the repeated cross-sectional National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal)
item.description:
Background: Human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and cervical screening have substantially reduced overall cervical cancer risk, but differences in uptake must be quantified to inform equitable access. This study aimed to provide population-level evidence of the impact of HPV vaccination on HPV types 16 and 18 (hereafter HPV-16/18) prevalence in England, Scotland, and Wales (hereafter Britain), and uptake of cervical cancer prevention interventions (ie, vaccination and screening), 15 years after the introduction of the vaccination programme in 2008.

Methods: We conducted the National Surveys of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), which are nationally representative, cross-sectional population surveys with individual-level data and HPV testing of biosamples. Data from Natsal-2 (1999-2001; before the vaccination programme was introduced, and included urine biosamples), Natsal-3 (2010-12; early in the vaccination programme, and included urine biosamples), and Natsal-4 (2022-24; after the vaccination programme was established, and included vaginal swab and urine biosamples) were analysed. Age-adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) for HPV-16/18 infection were estimated among women eligible for routine vaccination (born from Sept 1, 1995) compared with same-aged women before the vaccination programme was introduced. Combined Natsal-4 probability and non-probability data assessed factors associated with self-reported HPV vaccination and cervical screening.

Findings: Among 10 418 Natsal-4 women (aged 16-59 years), 1059 women in the probability sample group (aged 18-44 years) provided usable biosamples (Natsal-2 n=1849; Natsal-3 n=2407). HPV-16/18 prevalence was 86% lower (aPR 0·14, 95% CI 0·02-0·84) among those aged 18-29 years in Natsal-4 (1·6%, 95% CI 0·3-8·2) than in Natsal-2 (8·7%, 95% CI 6·7-11·3). All HPV-16/18 infections reported in Natsal-4 occurred in unvaccinated women. Of 733 routine vaccination-eligible women, 23·0% (95% CI 19·4-27·0) reported being unvaccinated. Among 3530 women (aged 25-59 years) eligible for cervical screening, 5·3% (95% CI 4·4-6·3) reported never attending screening. Non-uptake of vaccination and screening was higher among minority ethnic groups, religious groups, and those born outside the UK. Prevalence of high-risk, non-vaccine-preventable HPV (HPV 35, 39, 51, 56, and 59) infections was 4·9% (95% CI 3·7-6·4) in the total population, without any statistically significant differences between these subgroups. Women with higher-risk sexual behaviours were more likely to both be vaccinated and attend for screening.

Interpretation: Britain's HPV vaccination programme has driven a dramatic decline in HPV-16/18 prevalence and WHO cervical cancer elimination targets might be achievable overall if this is sustained. However, women from minority ethnic groups, religious groups, and those not born in the UK are less likely to be vaccinated and screened while remaining at risk. It is crucial to improve the reach of prevention interventions to more equitably reduce cervical cancer morbidity and mortality.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Comparing the single-item screen-cannabis (SIS-C) with brief cannabis screening questions for identifying cannabis use disorder
item.description:
Objectives: Compare performance of a validated Single-Item Screen-Cannabis (SIS-C) for cannabis use disorder (CUD) completed in primary care (PC) versus competed for research, and to compare the SIS-C (assessing past-year frequency of use) to alternative brief cannabis screens.

Methods: Adult PC patients who completed the SIS-C (3/28/2019-9/12/2019) in a Washington health system, were randomly sampled for a confidential survey. Participant responses (n = 1688) were linked to electronic health records (EHRs). CIDI-SAM, completed via survey, was the reference standard for any CUD and moderate-severe CUD. Screens included: (1) SIS-C completed in routine PC and documented in EHRs ("clinical SIS-C"); (2) SIS-C completed via survey not shared with providers ("research SIS-C"); (3) question assessing typical times-per-day of use completed via survey; and (4) composite measure combining frequency and times-per-day. Weighted analyses estimated sensitivity, specificity, and AUC of screens compared to CUD on the CIDI-SAM, estimating differences between AUCs (∆AUC) with confidence limits.

Results: Past-year CUD prevalence was 6.6% (1.9% moderate-severe). All screens demonstrated excellent discrimination for any and moderate-severe CUD (AUC≥ 0.80). Performance of the clinical SIS-C and research SIS-C did not differ for any CUD (ΔAUC -0.025 [95% CI -0.119-0.046]) while the clinical SIS-C performed slightly better for moderate-severe CUD (ΔAUC 0.024 [0.009-0.043]). The research SIS-C outperformed the times-per-day item, and the composite measure offered minimal improvement over frequency alone.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: The association of state cannabis legalization with polysubstance use disorders involving cannabis use disorder
item.description:
Objectives: To examine associations of state medical and recreational cannabis legalization (MCL, RCL) with polysubstance use disorders involving cannabis use disorder (CUD).

Methods: Using quasi-experimental difference-in-differences models with staggered adoption, we analyzed 2010-2022 Merative MarketScan Commercial Claims data for adults aged 18-64. Outcomes included: (1) prevalence of co-occurring CUD and alcohol, opioid, or tobacco use disorders (AUD, OUD, TUD) within the same quarter; (2) incident CUD diagnoses among patients with past-year AUD, OUD, or TUD; and (3) incident AUD, OUD, or TUD diagnoses among patients with past-year CUD. Incident cases were defined using a 6-month look-back period.

Findings: No significant associations were observed between cannabis legalization and prevalence of co-occurring CUD and AUD or TUD. Compared to states without cannabis legalization, RCL was associated with a 66.93% (coefficient=-8.26; 95%CI: -15.90,-0.62; P < 0.05) reduction in prevalence of co-occurring CUD and OUD. Among patients with past-year CUD, MCL and RCL were associated with 14.43% (coefficient=-0.14; 95%CI: -0.27,-0.010; P < 0.05) and 22.68% (coefficient=-0.22; 95%CI: -0.39,-0.045; P < 0.05) reductions in incident AUD diagnoses, and 20.73% (coefficient=-0.13; 95%CI: -0.25,-0.013; P < 0.05), and 44.61% (coefficient=-0.29; 95%CI: -0.48,-0.10; P < 0.01) reductions in incident OUD diagnoses, respectively. item.title: J Addict Med: When Intended Help Feels Harmful: A Qualitative Study on the Effects of Child Protective Services on Perinatal Individuals With Opioid Use Disorder
item.description:
Background: Federal and state policies have expanded child protective services (CPS) responsibilities related to prenatal substance exposure in response to the rise in opioid use disorder (OUD). However, little is known about how CPS involvement affects perinatal individuals with OUD. This study examines their perspectives on CPS processes and impacts.

Methods: We conducted semistructured interviews with 17 perinatal individuals with OUD enrolled in a larger study comparing the effectiveness of 2 support models for obstetric clinicians providing OUD treatment for pregnant and postpartum patients. Participants were asked about the effects of CPS reporting requirements on prenatal care, their understanding of CPS services, experiences with CPS, concerns about CPS involvement, and how information about CPS was communicated by obstetric providers, including hospitals. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed using Braun and Clarke thematic analysis approach.

Results: Seven themes emerged: (1) pervasive fear of CPS involvement; (2) poor communication from obstetric providers about CPS processes; (3) negative consequences of CPS reporting for individuals taking medications for OUD; (4) experiences of stigma and bias related to CPS; (5) positive CPS support for families; (6) harmful impacts of CPS involvement on health and wellbeing; and (7) the importance of self-advocacy among pregnant individuals with OUD.

Conclusions: Although CPS can offer support, its involvement often generates fear, stress, and stigmatization, producing unintended negative outcomes for perinatal individuals with OUD and their families. Trauma-informed implementation of CPS policies within health care systems and CPS agencies is needed to reduce adverse effects and improve patient experiences.

item.title: J Addict Med: Does Early Nonresponse to Buprenorphine Treatment Predict Mental Health and Quality of Life Outcomes?
item.description:
Objectives: In clinical trials of buprenorphine treatment for opioid use disorder (OUD), opioid use in the first 2-3 weeks of treatment is associated with later risk of return to use, and therefore might be useful for guiding stepped-care interventions to improve outcomes. However, little is known about the prognostic value of these early nonresponse indicators for patient-centered outcomes, such as mental health and quality of life (QoL). We aimed to examine the associations between early nonresponse to buprenorphine treatment and end-of-treatment depression and QoL.

Methods: Data were from 2 clinical trials of buprenorphine for OUD (Study 1, N=360; Study 2, N=202) that included the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) and 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) to assess QoL. Linear regressions examined associations between 2 previously identified indicators of early nonresponse (ie, any opioid use in weeks 1-2 and >1 day of use in weeks 1-3) and end-of-treatment BDI and SF-36 subscale scores, controlling for baseline levels. Trials were analyzed separately because of their different durations (12 vs. 16 wks).

Results: In one trial, >1 day of use in weeks 1-3 predicted worse SF-36 social functioning (b(SE)=-10.06 (3.51), P=0.004). We did not identify any other statistically significant associations between early nonresponse and mental health and QoL outcomes.

Conclusions: Early nonresponse to buprenorphine treatment showed a limited ability to predict later depression symptoms and QoL. Future research should identify early prognostic indicators that a patient may demonstrate poor mental health and QoL during buprenorphine treatment to improve patient-centered care.

item.title: J Addict Med: Chronic Hepatitis B and Delta Coinfection in a Person With Opioid Use Disorder: Missed Prevention Opportunities and Implications for Addiction Practice
item.description:
Objectives: People who inject drugs are disproportionately affected by hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis delta virus (HDV) infections. Missed HBV vaccination opportunities and delayed HDV testing in patients with substance use disorder can result in preventable liver disease.

Case summary: A 46-year-old White man with opioid use disorder (OUD), housing instability, chronic HBV, resolved hepatitis C virus infection, and injection drug use presented with newly decompensated liver disease. Review of prior records revealed documented HBV nonimmunity 9 years earlier during multiple outpatient encounters for OUD care and hepatitis C virus evaluation, yet no HBV vaccination was administered across 6 clinical visits. Following a lapse in care, he was diagnosed with chronic HBV 6 years later. An equivocal HDV antibody was identified the following year, but confirmatory HDV RNA testing was delayed by 2 more years, ultimately revealing high-level HDV viremia. He was initiated on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate/emtricitabine with significant HBV viral load reduction but required hepatology referral for decompensated liver disease and transplant consideration.

Conclusions/implications for addiction medicine: This case illustrates repeated missed opportunities for guideline-recommended HBV vaccination and timely HBV/HDV screening in a person with OUD, contributing to preventable decompensated liver disease. Addiction medicine settings are well positioned to deliver these recommended preventive services and to link patients to specialty care.

item.title: J Addict Med: Why 7-Hydroxymitragynine Restrictions Must Be Paired With Treatment Access
item.description:
The rapid proliferation of 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH), a potent opioid-active alkaloid derived from the kratom plant (Mitragyna speciosa), has prompted escalating regulatory responses from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), and numerous state legislatures. While legitimate safety concerns underlie these actions, the current trajectory of prohibition proceeds without adequate planning for the clinical disposition of individuals who have developed physical dependence on, or substance use problems related to, 7-OH-containing products. I argue that any regulatory framework restricting 7-OH should be paired with proactive expansion of low-barrier access to treatment, particularly buprenorphine, to mitigate foreseeable harms among affected users.

item.title: J Addict Med: Behavioral and Structural Factors Linking Psychological Trauma and Subsequent Drug Overdose: A Systematic Review
item.description:
Objectives: Psychological trauma is associated with increased risk of overdose. This review aims to identify, among people with a history of trauma, what factors contribute to their overdose risk, with a focus on intervening and modifiable exposures.

Methods: We searched Medline, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Embase for quantitative peer-reviewed studies on psychological trauma and subsequent unintentional overdose risk involving unregulated substances or opioids. Trauma types included interpersonal (violence, abuse, neglect, and discrimination) and noninterpersonal (disasters, accidents). Data were extracted using Covidence, and the risk of bias was assessed using the ROBINS-I/V2 tool.

Results: Thirty-five observational studies were included and had a low to moderate risk of bias. Both fatal and nonfatal overdoses, typically linked to polysubstance use, were observed. Lifetime nonfatal overdose prevalence ranged from 3% to 69% in high-risk groups. Members of vulnerable populations-such as people who inject drugs or engage in sex work, formerly incarcerated individuals, military veterans, and those living with mental health or substance use disorders-were at higher risk. Potentially modifiable factors included mental health conditions (depression, anxiety), substance use behaviors (eg, using alone, fentanyl exposure), treatment (opioid agonists), and social-environmental settings (homelessness, criminalization, barriers to access care, and social supports).

Conclusions: Cumulative exposure to childhood adversity, violence, and having post-traumatic stress disorder are associated with increased overdose risk in later life. Despite observational study limitations, psychological trauma, mental health issues, substance use behaviors, and social-structural conditions, including housing instability and violence exposure, often co-occur. Effective overdose prevention strategies must address both individual trauma and systemic inequities.

item.title: J Addict Med: Impact of Addiction Medicine Social Workers on Hospital Readmission
item.description:
Objectives: To assess whether involvement of a specialized social worker in inpatient addiction medicine consults was associated with lower 30-day all-cause readmission compared with consults without documented social work involvement.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using electronic health record data from a large safety-net hospital in Denver, Colorado, with an established addiction medicine consult service, focusing on adult hospitalizations with a completed addiction consult from January 1, 2023 to December 31, 2025. We used multivariable modified Poisson regression with generalized estimating equations to account for confounding and clustering among patients with multiple admissions, estimating the association between addiction medicine social work involvement and 30-day all-cause readmission. We examined robustness across subgroups, including patients receiving medications for addiction treatment and mutually exclusive substance use disorder categories.

Results: Among 5069 eligible hospitalizations, social work was involved in 2681 (53%). Adjusted models suggested lower readmission risk with social work involvement (adjusted risk ratio: 0.89; 95% CI: 0.78, 1.01). Among patients receiving medications for opioid use disorder, social work involvement was associated with a 22% reduction in readmission risk (adjusted risk ratio: 0.78; 95% CI: 0.63, 0.97), but no association was observed among those receiving medications for alcohol use disorder. The association varied by substance use disorder category.

Conclusions: Specialized social work involvement in inpatient addiction medicine consults was associated with lower 30-day readmission risk, particularly among patients who received medications for opioid use disorder. As hospitals expand inpatient addiction services, specialized social workers may be critical for supporting successful transitions to community care.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Subsidies and Behavioral Interventions to Increase Online Fruit and Vegetable Purchasing: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: The US population eats less than the recommended amounts of fruits and vegetables despite known health benefits. Innovative solutions to increase fruits and vegetables purchasing are needed.

Objective: To examine whether fruits and vegetables subsidies, choice architecture, and/or loss-framed text message reminders increase fruits and vegetables purchases in an online shopping store.

Design, setting, and participants: This 3-month pilot randomized clinical trial (October 24, 2024, and January 21, 2025) assessed individuals from the University of Pennsylvania Health System aged 30 to 70 years with a body mass index of 30 or greater and a hemoglobin A1c level greater than 8% who were comfortable shopping online and had a credit or debit card. Each participant participated for 3 months, but recruitment was rolling. The first participant was enrolled on October 24, 2024, and the last participant finished all study procedures on June 18, 2025. The last participant was enrolled January 27, 2025. The study used the online shopping platform Instacart.

Intervention: Participants were randomized to 1 of 5 arms: (1) control ($20 per month coupon on the study's online shopping platform), (2) subsidy ($160 per month for fruits and vegetables on the study's online shopping platform), (3) subsidy plus choice architecture (fruits and vegetables appear first on storefront), (4) subsidy plus salience (weekly loss-framed text messages about subsidy balance), or (5) subsidy plus salience plus choice architecture.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcome was total expenditures on fruits and vegetables on the study's online shopping platform. Secondary outcomes were (1) mean percentage of subsidy used across 3 months, (2) cumulative percentage of fruits and vegetables expenditures, and (3) change in HbA1c level. Analyses used either the intention-to-treat population or participants who activated their shopping memberships (per-protocol population).

Results: Of 1070 individuals assessed, 210 (129 [61.4%] female) were included in the study. Mean (SD) age of the study participants was 51.6 (10.8) years, and mean (SD) body mass index was 37.99 (7.28). Participants in the intention-to-treat group who received the subsidy spent a monthly mean of $92.52 (95% CI, $74.15-$110.90; P < .001) more on fruits and vegetables on the study's online shopping platform than the control group. Cumulative fruits and vegetables expenditure as a percentage of total expenditures was 21.47 percentage points (95% CI, 8.68-34.27 percentage points; P = .001) higher in the subsidy vs control arm. After 3 months, subsidy recipients vs control participants had a nonsignificant -0.28% (95% CI, -1.11% to 0.56%; P = .51) decrease in HbA1c level. In the per-protocol group, those receiving vs not receiving salience spent $18.83 (95% CI, $4.73-$32.92; P = .009) more on fruits and vegetables monthly. Choice architecture did not have a significant effect.

Conclusions and relevance: In this pilot randomized clinical trial of fruits and vegetables subsidies, choice architecture, and/or loss-framed text message reminders in an online store, providing a $160-monthly subsidy increased fruits and vegetables purchasing. Once participants activated memberships, weekly reminders of the subsidy balance but not choice architecture significantly increased fruits and vegetables spending.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Buprenorphine Use and State-Level Prior Authorization Changes in Medicaid
item.description:
Importance: To increase access to medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD), such as buprenorphine, several states have implemented laws limiting prior authorization requirements for MOUD in Medicaid plans.

Objective: To evaluate the association between state laws limiting preauthorization requirements for MOUD in Medicaid plans and buprenorphine use.

Design, setting, and participants: This repeated cross-sectional, difference-in-differences study examined buprenorphine prescriptions for Medicaid patients aged 15 to 64 years during January 1, 2014, to December 31, 2020. Data were derived from the IQVIA Longitudinal Prescription Database (including 94% of US prescriptions) and IQVIA Formulary Impact Analyzer (a pharmacy transactions database). Analyses included 13 treatment states that implemented laws during 2015 to 2019 and 25 control states that did not enact laws during 2014 to 2020. Data were analyzed between January 5 and May 11, 2026.

Exposure: Laws limiting prior authorization requirements.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes were monthly buprenorphine dispensing rates and initiation rates (number of patients with buprenorphine prescriptions and new prescriptions per 1000 Medicaid enrollees) and monthly dispensing gaps (days between the date prescriptions were written and dispensed). Subgroup analyses were conducted among states with high or low baseline prior authorization rejection rates, defined as the frequency of buprenorphine prescription rejection due to prior authorization requirements during the 12 months before law implementation (treatment states) or during 2014 (control states).

Results: Sample sizes varied by outcome: dispensing rate, 12 697 583 prescriptions for 652 035 patients (mean [SD] age at the time of a claim, 37.6 [9.5] years; 327 493 female [50.2%]), initiation rate, 723 592 new prescriptions for 588 940 patients (mean [SD] age, 36.3 [9.6] years; 295 012 female [50.1%]), and dispensing gap, 9 495 547 prescriptions for 516 790 patients (mean [SD] age, 37.7 [9.5]; 263 366 female [51.0%]). Laws were not associated with changes in the dispensing rate (0.11 patients per 1000; 95% CI, -0.30 to 0.52 patients per 1000), initiation rate (0.01 new patients per 1000; 95% CI, -0.04 to 0.06 new patients per 1000), or dispensing gap (-0.45 days; 95% CI, -0.97 to 0.08 days). Among states with high baseline prior authorization rejection rates, laws were associated with increases in the dispensing rate (0.29 patients per 1000; 95% CI, 0.07-0.51 patients per 1000) and initiation rate (0.06 new patients per 1000; 95% CI, 0.03-0.10 new patients per 1000) and with decreases in the dispensing gap (-0.91 days; 95% CI, -1.76 to -0.05 days).

Conclusions and relevance: This repeated cross-sectional study found that laws limiting prior authorization requirements for MOUD were only associated with increased buprenorphine dispensing, increased initiation, and timelier buprenorphine receipt when prior authorization requirements were frequent barriers to access.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Deimplementing Race Adjustment in Clinical Algorithms and Decision Tools
item.description:
Importance: Many clinical decision support tools (CDSTs) incorporate race adjustment to tailor treatment based on a patient's race and ethnicity, contributing to racial and ethnic disparities in care. Mounting calls for race adjustment removal have resulted in some progress, yet the use of race adjustment in medicine persists.

Objective: To explore the processes, barriers, and facilitators to the implementation of race adjustment removal from 16 CDSTs and clinical information systems.

Design, setting, and participants: This qualitative study used the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) 2.0 to conduct virtual semistructured interviews with clinicians from different specialties at a multihospital academic health system from September 1, 2023, to August 31, 2024. An optional demographics survey was also sent to participants.

Main outcomes and measures: Patterns identified through thematic analysis informed by the CFIR 2.0 framework.

Results: Of the 44 identified clinicians, 32 (72.7%) completed an interview across 16 specialties. Of the 26 participants who reported their demographics, 14 (53.8%) were female, 6 (23.1%) were Asian, 1 (3.8%) were Hispanic or Latinx, 6 (23.1%) were non-Hispanic Black or African American, 13 (50%) were non-Hispanic White, 1 (3.8%) were multiracial or multiethnic, and 2 (7.9%) were other races or ethnicities (any other race or ethnicity). Thematic analysis of the interviews highlighted 5 generalizable themes: (1) clinicians varied greatly in their perceptions of race and race adjustment; (2) resistance, indifference, and unawareness remain key barriers to deimplementing race-based medicine; (3) race adjustment often serves as a harbinger of broader challenges with CDSTs; (4) consequences of race adjustment removal efforts remain understudied; and (5) national medical societies and multidisciplinary engagement are critical to overcoming implementation barriers.

Conclusions and relevance: In this qualitative study, cross-specialty perspectives yielded several critical barriers to deimplementing race adjustment in clinical medicine, alongside the identification of strategies required to drive change.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Bone Mineral Density, FRAX Score, and Fracture Risk in Asian Adults With Type 2 Diabetes
item.description:
Importance: The recommendation of reducing the femoral neck (FN) bone mineral density (BMD) T score by 0.5 for fracture risk assessment in type 2 diabetes (T2D) is based primarily on data from White populations. Generalizability to Asian populations is unclear.

Objective: To evaluate associations of BMD and Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX) scores with fracture risk in Asians with T2D and the difference in FN BMD T score between those with vs without T2D at equal hip fracture risk.

Design, setting, and participants: This prospective cohort study using data from the Hong Kong Osteoporosis Study included adults 40 years of age or older with or without T2D recruited between 1995 and 2010. Data were captured until January 15, 2024, and analyzed in April 2025.

Exposures: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry-measured BMD T scores at the lumbar spine, FN, and total hip, and FRAX scores calculated using clinical risk factors and FN BMD.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcomes were hip fracture and major osteoporotic fracture (MOF). Cox proportional hazards models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs.

Results: This cohort study consisted of 5817 adults (mean [SD] age, 61.3 [11.9] years; 4116 [70.76%] women). Of 629 participants with T2D, 107 (17.01%) experienced hip fractures, and 152 (24.17%) experienced MOFs during a mean (SD) follow-up period of 12.1 (7.2) years. HRs adjusted for age and sex per unit decrease in FN BMD T score were 1.57 (95% CI, 1.28-1.93) for hip fracture and 1.45 (95% CI, 1.22-1.72) for MOF. Higher FRAX score was also associated with an increased risk of hip fracture (HR, 1.07 [95% CI, 1.05-1.09] and MOF (HR, 1.05 [95% CI, 1.04-1.06]) in people with T2D. In addition, fracture incidence rates were higher in people with T2D than in those without T2D, with hip fracture rates of 13.27 vs 3.77 per 1000 person-years, respectively, and MOF rates of 19.92 vs 7.64 per 1000 person-years, respectively. For the same hip fracture risk at the same age, women with T2D had a higher FN BMD T score of 1.34 (95% CI, 0.69-1.98) and men of 0.47 (95% CI, 0.05-0.89) than those without T2D.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 5817 adults, BMD T score and FRAX score were associated with increased fracture risk in a population of Asian people with T2D. The magnitude of downward adjustment in BMD T score in Asians with T2D requires further external validation.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Parental Consent Requirements and Federally Funded Reproductive Health Care Among Texas Adolescents
item.description:
Importance: Since the 1970s, the federal Title X program has guaranteed confidential reproductive health care to young people in the US. A December 2022 court ruling, Alexander R. Deanda v Xavier Becerra et al, determined that Title X's confidentiality guarantees violated Texas state law regarding parental rights, thereby requiring parental consent for minors' contraceptive care.

Objective: To examine changes in patient volume, patient characteristics, and health care services received at Title X-funded health centers among Texas minors aged 17 years or younger compared with people aged 18 years in 2023 following implementation of the 2022 Deanda ruling.

Design, setting, and participants: This observational cohort study used a quasi-experimental pre-post design. The study included all visits that occurred between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2023, among patients aged 18 years or younger receiving services at Title X-funded health centers in Texas. Data were analyzed between December 2024 and August 2026.

Exposure: Implementation in January 2023 of parental consent for contraception.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcome was the relative change in the number of patients and visits for minors (vs people aged 18 years) in the 1 year after the Deanda decision (2023) compared with the prior year (2022). Secondary outcomes included changes in the demographic profile of patients and in services received (eg, prescription contraception, leaving the visit with only condoms, sexually transmitted infection testing, or pregnancy testing). This study used difference-in-differences (DiD) Poisson regression analysis.

Results: Overall, 33 214 individuals (mean [SD] age, 16.3 [1.9] years; 27 040 female [81.4%]) were included in the analysis: 21 687 were aged 17 years or younger and 11 527 were aged 18 years. The number of individual minors decreased from 11 496 to 10 191 between 2022 and 2023 (percentage change, -11.4% [95% CI, -13.7% to -9.0%]); there was no statistically significant change among people aged 18 years (n = 5733 in 2022 and 5794 in 2023; percentage change, 1.1% [95% CI, -2.6% to 4.8%]). In DiD models, the 2022 to 2023 change in patient volume among minors was 9% lower relative to the corresponding change among people aged 18 years (multiplicative DiD, 0.91 [95% CI, 0.82 to 1.00]; P = .05). Compared with 2022, there were significantly fewer visits in 2023 among minors who were male compared with female (percentage change, -24.4% [95% CI, -28.7% to -20.0%] vs -7.4% [95% CI, -10.2% to -4.7%]; P < .001) and had limited English language proficiency compared with English proficiency (percentage change, -22.2% [95% CI, -26.5% to -17.9%] vs -7.7% [95% CI, -10.6% to -4.9%]; P < .001). There were no statistically significant differences in services received between minors and people aged 18 years before vs after the ruling.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, Texas minors' use of Title X-funded services decreased relative to people aged 18 years following the 2023 implementation of required parental consent for contraception. At a time when confidentiality protections for adolescents are under threat, these findings highlight how parental consent requirements interfere with access to reproductive health care.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Prediction of Acetaminophen-Induced Hepatotoxicity in Acetylcysteine-Treated Patients Using Routine Admission Biomarkers
item.description:
Study objective: Some acetaminophen-overdose patients develop hepatotoxicity despite acetylcysteine treatment. Established tools struggle to prospectively identify subsequent toxicity. We developed a model using only routine admission biomarkers to identify acetylcysteine-treated patients at highest risk and compared it with the current benchmark, the acetaminophen-aminotransferase multiplication product (AT product).

Methods: Retrospective cohort study of acetaminophen overdose admissions aged 12 years and older (International Classification of Diseases 10th revision code of T39.1) with alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ≤1,000 U/L at admission from 3 UK hospitals (2008-2024). We fitted elastic-net logistic models stratified by presentation ALT. The outcome was peak ALT >1,000 U/L. Performance was assessed on a 25% held-out test set and benchmarked against the AT product >1,500.

Results: Of 4,705 admissions, 119 (2.5%) developed hepatotoxicity. The model used 7 routine blood tests, 4 per stratum. At presentation, those with ALT ≤50 U/L, acetaminophen, sodium, potassium, and lymphocyte count remained in the model. In those with ALT 51 to 1,000 U/L at presentation, ALT, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lymphocyte count were used. In the test set (n=1,175), it achieved an area under the curve of 0.93 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.89 to 0.97) versus 0.82 (0.72 to 0.91) for the AT product (paired difference 0.11; 95% CI 0.01 to 0.22; P=.03), with higher specificity and a higher positive likelihood ratio at every matched sensitivity. The model had a specificity of 82.5%, whereas an AT product > 1,500 had a specificity of 62.6%. The model positive likelihood ratio was 5.1 versus 2.4 for the AT product, with half the number of false-positive escalations (171 versus 365 per 1,000 patients).

Conclusion: A stratified model using only routine admission biomarkers (the Edinburgh Risk Score) identifies acetylcysteine-treated patients at the highest residual hepatotoxicity risk, outperforming the AT product >1,500 across decision thresholds, supporting selection for intensified therapy.

item.description:
Study objective: Hypothermic temperature control has not consistently demonstrated a neuroprotective effect, resulting in heterogeneity of use in clinical practice. We evaluated temperature control quality across 4 institutions and its association with clinical outcomes.

Methods: Retrospective analysis of institutional registry data collected between 2021 and 2024 in survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with Glasgow Coma Scale Motor score less than 6 from 4 academic centers with established cardiac arrest programs. Eligible patients included those 18 years of age or older, treated with hypothermic temperature control (33-36°C) using a feedback-controlled device, and admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU). A temperature control quality score (0-6) was assigned for each patient. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. The secondary outcome was good neurologic outcome at hospital discharge, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) score of 1-2. Univariable and multivariable logistic regressions quantified the relationship between quality of temperature control, as an ordinal variable, and outcomes.

Results: Among 356 included patients, most were male (N=224, 62.9%) with mean (standard deviation [SD]) age 58.1 (15.2) years. Most suffered a nonshockable arrest (N=262, 73.6%) and did not receive layperson CPR (N=225, 63.2%). Median [IQR] Pittsburgh Cardiac Arrest Category score was 4 [3,4], mean (SD) lactate 9.1 (4.1) mmol/L, and pH 7.09 (0.17). Median [IQR] preinduction time was 2.3 [1.5 to 3.5] hours and 150 (42.1%) were treated with early neuromuscular blockade. Adjusting for confounders in the multivariable model, an increase of one-point in the temperature control quality score was associated with improved survival at hospital discharge (odds ratio [OR] 1.32; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.07 to 1.64). A one-point increase in the quality score also resulted in a shift towards lower (improved) CPC score (OR 1.28; 95% CI, 0.05 to 1.55). The direction of effect was consistent across all centers.

Conclusion: In unresponsive survivors of OHCA, an increase in temperature control quality was associated with improved survival and better neurologic outcome; however, confounding by site, injury severity, or perceived prognosis is possible. Lack of temperature control parameter standardization may influence efficacy and practice variability within pragmatic-design clinical trials possibly contributed to neutral trial results. Prospective trials evaluating the importance of temperature control quality and the population most likely to benefit from hypothermic temperature control are essential.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Frequency and Causes of Waveform Capnography Failure After Successful Emergency Tracheal Intubation
item.description:
Study objective: Multidisciplinary guidelines recommend waveform capnography as the preferred method for determining endotracheal tube location after intubation and advise immediate tube removal when the waveform is absent or inadequate unless a fault can be immediately identified and corrected. Because capnography depends on several components that can each fail, an absent waveform does not always indicate an esophageal tube, and removing a correctly placed tube exposes a critically ill patient to the risks of reintubation. How often waveform capnography fails despite correct tracheal placement has been estimated only from trials of colorimetric detectors in populations with high proportions of cardiac arrest, and the causes have not been described.

Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of a prospectively collected continuous quality improvement database of emergency intubations at an urban, safety-net hospital, including patients aged ≥14 years intubated between January 1, 2022, and April 21, 2025. Trained observers collected intubation data in real time, and the intubating physician completed a structured form after each procedure. The primary outcome was CO2 waveform failure following successful tracheal intubation. Secondary outcomes were the reported cause of failure and whether the tube was removed.

Results: Of 2,875 successful tracheal intubation procedures, 124 (4.3%; 95% confidence interval 3.6 to 5.1%) had CO2 waveform failure despite the tube being located in the trachea. Human error accounted for 83 events (67%), nearly all of which were from the CO2 sampling line not being connected to the bag or the monitor (82 events, 66%). Identified equipment failure accounted for 11 events (9%). The cause was undetermined in 33 events (27%), including 30 (24%) in which the failure was never explained despite confirmed tracheal placement and 3 in which the cause was not formally categorized. The endotracheal tube was removed because of the absent waveform in 1 event (1%).

Conclusion: CO2 waveform failure occurred in approximately 4% of successful intubation procedures.

item.title: JAMA: Prehospital Fluid Resuscitation for Patients With Suspected Sepsis: The PITSTOP-Fluids Factorial Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Early resuscitation with intravenous fluids is recommended for patients with sepsis.

Objective: To determine the effect of liberal vs more conservative fluid resuscitation strategies in the ambulance on mortality among patients with suspected sepsis.

Design, setting, and participants: Multicenter, 2 × 2 factorial randomized clinical trial conducted by 4 paramedic services and their destination hospitals in Ontario, Canada. Participants were adults with suspected sepsis, defined as suspected infection, fever (≥38.0 °C), and hypotension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] <100 mm Hg), and obtainable intravenous access. Patients were enrolled between March 23, 2020, and August 20, 2025, with last follow-up in December 2025.

Intervention: Patients were randomized to receive liberal fluids (up to 2 L of normal saline regardless of subsequent SBP) or usual care (fluids only when SBP <90 mm Hg and stopped when SBP ≥100 mm Hg) during prehospital care and until transfer of care in the emergency department. (Patients were additionally randomized to receive ceftriaxone vs placebo; analysis of which is reported separately.).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was hospital mortality, defined as death prior to hospital discharge up to day 90. There were 17 secondary outcomes, including all-cause mortality at 90 days, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, mechanical ventilation, vasopressor therapy, dialysis, and total fluids infused within 24 hours of hospital arrival.

Results: Among 1686 randomized patients, 1669 were eligible and 1646 were included in the primary outcome analysis (830 in the liberal fluids group and 816 in the usual fluids group). The median age of patients was 76 (IQR, 63-85) years and 938 (57.0%) were male. Most patients in both groups received a fluid bolus (826/848 [97.4%] in the liberal fluids group; 700/821 [85.3%] in the usual fluids group) during transport, but patients in the liberal fluids group received a larger volume (median, 1500 mL [IQR, 1000-2000 mL]) vs 500 mL [IQR, 175-800 mL] in the usual fluids group; difference, 910.1 mL [95% CI, 857.3-962.9 mL]). Hospital mortality was 149/830 (18.0%) in the liberal fluids group and 149/816 (18.3%) in the usual fluids group (risk ratio, 0.98 [95% CI, 0.80-1.20]; unadjusted risk difference, -0.3 [95% CI, -4.0 to 3.4]; P = .82). Among the 17 secondary outcomes, all were similar between groups. Adverse events, including pulmonary edema during transport, were infrequent in both groups.

Conclusions and relevance: A more liberal fluid resuscitation strategy for the prehospital management of patients with suspected sepsis did not reduce mortality compared with more restrictive usual care.

item.description:
Importance: Early treatment with antibiotics is considered an important intervention to reduce mortality for patients with sepsis.

Objective: To determine the effect of earlier treatment with antibiotics in the ambulance on 90-day mortality compared with usual treatment in the emergency department.

Design, setting, and participants: This multicenter, 2 × 2 factorial randomized, placebo-controlled trial was conducted among 4 paramedic services and their destination hospitals in Ontario, Canada. Participants were adults with suspected sepsis, defined as suspected infection, fever (≥38.0 °C), and hypotension (systolic blood pressure <100 mm Hg). Patients were enrolled between March 23, 2020, and August 20, 2025, with final follow-up in December 2025.

Interventions: Patients were randomized to receive 1 g of intramuscular ceftriaxone or placebo (and to receive liberal fluids vs usual fluids; reported separately) during prehospital care in the ambulance. All patients could receive open-label antibiotics in the emergency department.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was hospital mortality, defined as death prior to hospital discharge to day 90. There were 17 secondary outcomes, including all-cause mortality at 90 days, hospitalization, intensive care unit admission, use of mechanical ventilation, use of dialysis, positive culture results, and antibiotics within 24 hours of hospital arrival.

Results: Among 2091 randomized patients, 2048 were eligible for the primary analysis, with 1026 randomized to receive ceftriaxone and 1022 randomized to receive placebo. The median (IQR) age of patients was 75 (62-85) years and 1162 (56.7%) were males. The mean (SD) time from paramedic arrival at patient to administration of study drug was 37 (36) minutes in the ceftriaxone group and 39 (55) minutes in the placebo group. Most patients (735 of 795 [92.5%] in the ceftriaxone group and 730 of 792 [92.2%] in placebo group) were treated with antibiotics in the hospital after a mean (SD) of 247.3 (207.7) minutes after paramedic arrival among patients in the ceftriaxone group and 252.8 (218.0) minutes among the placebo group. The rate of hospital mortality was 182 of 1009 (18.0%) in the ceftriaxone group and 186 of 1011 (18.4%) in the placebo group (risk ratio, 0.97 [95% CI, 0.81-1.17]; P = .77). Of 17 secondary outcomes, all were similar between the groups.

Conclusions and relevance: Among patients with suspected sepsis on evaluation by paramedics, earlier treatment with antibiotics in the ambulance did not reduce mortality compared with usual care provided in the emergency department.

item.title: Crit Care: The sepsis trial landscape: a domain-specific systematic review and meta-analysis of adult sepsis randomized controlled trials
item.description:
Background: Despite decades of sepsis randomized clinical trials (RCTs), few therapeutic interventions have demonstrated reproducible mortality benefit. Whether this phenomenon reflects failure of individual therapies or broader limitations in sepsis RCT design remains unclear. We hypothesized that examining clinically distinct treatment domains would reveal differences in mortality effect estimates while identifying recurrent trial-design limitations shared across domains. Therefore, we performed a domain-specific meta-analysis of adult sepsis RCTs and evaluated the distribution of mortality effect estimates across treatment domains using a complementary landscape analysis framework and structured trial-design analysis.

Methods: We conducted a meta-analysis of adult sepsis and septic shock RCTs published between 2000 and 2025 (PROSPERO CRD420261289221). Using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL, two reviewers screened studies and extracted data. Trials were grouped into six treatment domains: initial resuscitation interventions, intravenous fluid quantity, intravenous fluid type, vasopressors, corticosteroids, and vitamin C-based therapies. Separate random-effects meta-analyses estimated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We also performed a complementary landscape analysis using Python to evaluate the distribution of mortality effect estimates relative to study sample size, as well as a structured thematic analysis to identify recurrent trial design constraints across treatment domains.

Results: Across 62 RCTs (n = 36,739), pooled mortality effects demonstrated no mortality benefit across each of the six treatment domains: resuscitation interventions (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77-1.01), intravenous fluid quantity (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88-1.05), intravenous fluid type (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89-1.01), vasopressors (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88-1.07), corticosteroids (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.84-1.00), and vitamin C-based therapies (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.83-1.09). A landscape analysis showed wider dispersion of mortality effect estimates among smaller trials, whereas larger trial estimates generally clustered near the null. A structured thematic analysis using a prespecified trial-constraint framework identified recurrent design limitations across treatment domains, including delayed intervention timing, biologic and clinical heterogeneity, treatment contamination, and trial design and infrastructure constraints.

Conclusions: Across the six prespecified treatment domains in sepsis, RCTs have not demonstrated consistent reductions in mortality. Recurrent trial-design limitations were common across treatment domains and may inform interpretation and future trial design.
