item.title: JAMA: Intramuscular Olanzapine or Droperidol for Acute Behavioral Disturbance in Children and Adolescents: The PEAChY-M Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Acute behavioral disturbance is a high-risk emergency department presentation. There is limited evidence for the comparative effectiveness of intramuscular sedative medications in children and adolescents, which may be required when there is imminent risk of serious harm due to agitation.

Objective: To determine whether olanzapine is more effective than droperidol intramuscularly in achieving behavioral containment.

Design, setting, and participants: This investigator-initiated, open-label, multicenter, superiority, randomized clinical trial recruited children and adolescents aged 9 to 17 years presenting to 10 Australian emergency departments with acute behavioral disturbance clinically deemed to require intramuscular medication from November 8, 2021, to February 16, 2026. The last participant follow-up occurred on March 17, 2026. Data were analyzed from April 15 to 27, 2026.

Interventions: Participants were randomly assigned to a single weight-based dose of olanzapine or droperidol (<40 kg, 5 mg; ≥40 kg, 10 mg).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was successful sedation (Sedation Assessment Tool score ≤0) without the need for additional sedatives 1 hour after randomization. A range of secondary outcomes, including adverse events, were assessed.

Results: Of 348 recruited individuals (mean [IQR] age, 14.9 [13.6-16.1] years; 215 [62%] female; 75 Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander individuals), 176 were assigned to olanzapine and 172 to droperidol. Of those randomized, 117 individuals (66%) in the olanzapine group and 121 individuals (70%) in the droperidol group were administered their study medication within 30 minutes of randomization. Successful sedation without the requirement for additional sedatives occurred in 89 individuals (53%) in the olanzapine group and 104 individuals (62%) in the droperidol group. No evidence of superiority was observed (adjusted risk difference, -8.3% [95% CI, -18.6% to 2.1%]; P = .12). One serious adverse event (apnea) occurred in the olanzapine group.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial in children and adolescents presenting to the emergency department with behavioral disturbance, intramuscular olanzapine did not result in a clinically meaningfully greater proportion achieving successful sedation compared with droperidol. The limited effectiveness observed with both medications highlights the need for more effective pharmacological and nonpharmacological management strategies.

item.title: Chest: Pulmonary Function Estimation from Opportunistic Chest CT Using a Hybrid Image-plus-Quantitative-Feature Deep Learning Model
item.description:
Background: Spirometry is underused and most airflow obstruction remains undiagnosed. Chest CT acquired for lung cancer screening contains anatomical and densitometric information that may proxy lung function.

Research question: Can a deep learning model combining volumetric CT with CT-derived quantitative features estimate spirometric parameters and detect abnormal spirometry in independent external cohorts without retraining?

Study design and methods: A three-dimensional convolutional neural network trained on 10,371 low-dose CT reconstructions from 5,975 National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) participants was fused with 20 lung densitometry and tracheal geometry features to predict FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC. The frozen model was applied to an External Lung Cancer Screening Cohort (ELCSC, n = 268) and COPDGene (n = 10,302 scans). Ablation, two spirometric-pattern subgroups and prevalence-conditional predictive values were also evaluated. Reference spirometry was pre-bronchodilator in NLST and post-bronchodilator in COPDGene. Abnormal spirometry (FEV1/FVC < 0.70, FEV1 < 80% or FVC < 80% predicted) was assessed with sensitivity, specificity and AUROC, and agreement with the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC).

Results: The model detected abnormal spirometry with AUROC 0.898 (sensitivity 89.9%, specificity 66.1%) in the ELCSC and AUROC 0.913 (sensitivity 66.9%, specificity 96.3%) in COPDGene, with CCCs of 0.80-0.88 for FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC. In held-out development data, CCCs were 0.86/0.85/0.71 (full model) versus 0.83/0.82/0.50 image-only and 0.55/0.65/0.35 feature-only. Agreement was lower, with systematic overestimation, in a COPD subgroup (FEV1/FVC < 0.70; CCC 0.62) and in a low-FVC, preserved-ratio pattern (CCC 0.70-0.78).

Interpretation: The model estimates spirometric parameters and detects abnormal spirometry across independent cohorts without retraining, with different sensitivity-specificity profiles at the same decision rule. It shows promise for opportunistic assessment of existing CT scans, but referral performance varies by population and prospective utility is unproven.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: The national diagnostic landscape of acute pelvic and lower abdominal pain in reproductive-age women presenting to U.S. emergency departments
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Study objective: To characterize the national distribution of emergency department (ED) diagnoses among reproductive-age women presenting with pelvic or lower abdominal pain and describe the frequency of selected time-sensitive diagnoses and ED disposition.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of the National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey (NHAMCS) ED public-use files from 2018 through 2022. We included female patients aged 18 to 49 years whose first-listed reason for visit was pelvic pain (reason-for-visit code 17751) or lower-abdominal pain (15452), excluding trauma-related visits. The primary outcome was the distribution of the first-listed ED diagnosis. Secondary outcomes included selected time-sensitive diagnoses, disposition, and documented diagnostic evaluation and treatment. Analyses incorporated NHAMCS survey weights, strata, and primary sampling units to generate nationally representative estimates.

Results: Among 86,864 sampled ED visits, 411 met the primary cohort definition, representing an estimated 637,594 visits annually (95% CI, 536,466-738,723). A nonspecific abdominal or pelvic pain diagnosis was the most common first-listed diagnosis (42.5%; 95% CI, 36.4%-48.9%), followed by urinary tract infection (11.1%) and ovarian cyst (8.5%). Most other individual time-sensitive diagnoses were statistically unreliable because of small sampled counts. Overall, 91.3% of visits resulted in discharge and 6.9% in admission. Diagnostic services were ordered or provided in 97.9% of visits. Visits receiving a nonspecific diagnosis had a similar mean number of diagnostic services as visits receiving another coded diagnosis (5.7 vs 5.7; P = .89) and were more likely to include imaging (78.6% vs 62.1%; difference, 16.5 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.2-28.8; P = .009). In a sensitivity cohort in which pelvic or lower-abdominal pain appeared in any reason-for-visit field (n = 740), the principal pattern persisted, with nonspecific diagnoses accounting for 31.4% of visits.

Conclusions: Among reproductive-age women presenting to U.S. EDs with pelvic or lower abdominal pain, nonspecific abdominal or pelvic pain was the most common final diagnosis, while individual time-sensitive diagnoses were uncommon and most patients were discharged. The frequent use of documented diagnostic services among visits ending in a nonspecific diagnosis suggests that diagnostic uncertainty often persists despite substantial ED evaluation. These national estimates provide epidemiologic context for a diagnostically challenging ED presentation and may inform future research in diagnostic reasoning, imaging, and clinical decision support.

item.title: Ann Intern Med: Screening for Prostate Cancer : A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
item.description:
Background: Previous reviews on prostate cancer screening relied on ongoing trials of invitations to screening with prostate-specific antigen (PSA), which may lack sufficient follow-up for mortality and overdiagnosis. Other screening tests with higher specificity may improve the benefit-harm profile.

Purpose: To examine benefits and harms of screening versus no screening or usual care.

Data sources: MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (2014 to 28 January 2026); reviews and included studies for studies published before 2014.

Study selection: Paired reviewers identified randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective nonrandomized studies. Benefit outcomes relied on data reported by age when possible.

Data extraction: Paired reviewers extracted data and assessed risk of bias. Random-effects meta-analysis was conducted with investigation of heterogeneity; assessment of certainty of evidence used the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) approach with decision thresholds as the targets of certainty.

Data synthesis: Thirteen RCTs (n = 792 034; 8 from a multisite European trial, and 1 for harms only) and 3 uncontrolled cohort studies (n = 5593; all for harms) were included. All RCTs compared invitations to PSA-based screening versus no invitation. At 20 years' follow-up, among 1000 men who were invited to multiple rounds of PSA-based screening every 2 to 4 years starting at age 55 to 69 years (mean, 62 years), there was likely a reduction in prostate cancer mortality (≥2 fewer) and metastatic cancer incidence (≥6 fewer) at the expense of prostate cancer overdiagnosis (≥20 cases) and false positives (≥150 cases) (all moderate certainty). Findings for ages 50 to 54 years were less certain. An invitation to 1 round of screening or to start screening at age 70 to 74 years may not lead to important benefit or harm (low to moderate certainty).

Limitation: Findings may differ for populations at elevated risk.

Conclusion: There was low- to very-low-certainty evidence of no important benefit for a 1-time invitation to PSA screening. Moderate-certainty evidence showed benefit with multiple invitations to PSA-based screening starting at age 55 to 69 years, although with harm from overdiagnosis and false positives.

item.description:
Background: Reducing racial mortality disparities remains a central goal of U.S. health policy, and progress varies by cause of death.

Objective: To quantify cause-specific contributions to changes in excess mortality rate (EMR) among Black versus White populations.

Design: Cross-sectional temporal analyses.

Setting: Mortality data.

Participants: Non-Hispanic Black and non-Hispanic White decedents stratified by sex and age at death (<20, <65, or ≥65 years).

Measurements: EMRs among Black versus White populations in 1993 and 2023 for all-cause and 24 causes of death, calculated as differences in age-standardized mortality rates, and changes in EMRs, calculated by subtracting the 2023 EMR from the 1993 EMR with cause-specific contribution to all-cause EMR reduction, expressed as a percentage.

Results: In 2023, all-cause EMR for Black versus White persons decreased by 56% (288.5 deaths per 100 000 person-years) for males and by 68% (175.8 deaths per 100 000 person-years) for females compared with 1993. Among males, reductions were predominantly driven by cancer (38.2% [95% CI, 36.4% to 40.0%]), HIV (17.5% [CI, 17.0% to 18.1%]), and heart disease (12.3% [CI, 10.2% to 14.4%]); among females, primary drivers were heart disease (31.9% [CI, 29.8% to 34.0%]), cancer (13.0% [CI, 11.3% to 14.8%]), and HIV (7.9% [CI, 7.5% to 8.3%]). Further gains were limited by lower progress or worsening disparities in maternal death; nephritis and accidents and adverse effects in both sexes; and homicide and legal intervention, diabetes, hypertension without heart disease, and cerebrovascular diseases (≥65 years) in males. Over time, cancer fell from the leading contributor to sixth among males and from second to fifth among females, whereas HIV declined from fourth or fifth to tenth in both sexes as contributors to the Black-White mortality gap.

Limitation: The analysis compared 1993 and 2023, although peak EMR years varied by cause of death, and alternative periods could yield different cause-specific contributions.

Conclusion: Reductions in EMR among Black versus White populations were driven by improvements in mortality from major causes. Shifting drivers of the racial mortality gap highlight priorities for further progress.

Objective: To determine whether less intensive follow-up of small pulmonary nodules is noninferior to more intensive follow-up.

Design: Unblinded, cluster randomized, pragmatic comparative effectiveness trial. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02623712).

Setting: 24 clusters of U.S. hospitals and health care systems.

Participants: 34 686 patients with a new pulmonary nodule measuring 15 mm or less, detected incidentally or by screening.

Intervention: Follow-up protocols were modeled on current and prior recommendations from the Fleischner Society and the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS). Each cluster was randomly assigned to the less or more intensive follow-up protocol.

Measurements: The primary outcome was the proportion of lung cancers measuring more than 20 mm at diagnosis. Analyses were conducted using mixed-effects logistic regression. The prespecified noninferiority margin was 5 percentage points.

Results: A total of 34 686 participants (50.8% women) were enrolled, with a mean age of 64.5 years (SD, 11.7). Lung cancer was diagnosed within 27 months of nodule identification in 273 of 17 841 participants (1.5%) in the less intensive group and 231 of 16 845 (1.4%) in the more intensive group. Among participants with lung cancer with available data, 97 of 267 (36.3%) in the less intensive group and 62 of 224 (27.7%) in the more intensive group had cancers larger than 20 mm at diagnosis. After adjustment, more lung cancers larger than 20 mm were identified with less intensive screening (7 percentage points [95% CI, -2.0 to 15.9 percentage points]), exceeding the noninferiority margin but not statistically significant.

Limitations: Suboptimal adherence, limited power, and residual confounding.

Conclusion: Small, malignant pulmonary nodules frequently progress during follow-up. Although neither follow-up strategy was clearly superior, these data raise concerns about the less intensive recommendations for follow-up of small nodules.

item.title: JAMA: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: A Review
item.description:
Importance: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is defined as left ventricular hypertrophy of greater than 15 mm in any part of the left ventricular wall in the absence of valvular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, or other chronic conditions causing severe left ventricular hypertrophy such as uncontrolled hypertension or cardiac amyloidosis. Most people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have a normal lifespan; however, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is associated with a 0.8% annual incidence of sudden cardiac death.

Observations: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy affects an estimated 0.2% of people worldwide (including more than 600 000 people in the US) and is typically diagnosed with echocardiography. Approximately 35% to 40% of patients report effort-related dyspnea, chest pain or pressure, or lightheadedness. Approximately 30% to 40% of people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy have a pathogenic gene variant that encodes for cardiac sarcomere proteins (predominantly myosin binding protein C, myosin heavy chain, and troponin). Other patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy may have a polygenic predisposition and/or nongenetic risk factors. The sarcomeric gene variants cause hypercontractility and delayed relaxation of the cardiac sarcomere, which characterizes the underlying pathophysiologic problem in people with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Approximately 60% to 70% of patients have obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, characterized by dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction due to basal septal hypertrophy. The remainder do not have outflow tract obstruction and, therefore, have nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy should participate in regular low- to moderate-intensity physical activity (such as brisk walking, jogging) as part of a healthy lifestyle. Medical therapies such as β-blockers (eg, metoprolol, bisoprolol, nadolol) and nondihydropyridine-class calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil or diltiazem) are first-line medical therapy for patients with symptoms due to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. If first-line therapies do not relieve symptoms, alternative treatments include disopyramide, which improves symptoms in approximately 60% of patients, cardiac myosin inhibitors (mavacamten or aficamten), which improve symptoms in approximately 70% to 80% of patients, or procedures to thin the septal wall of the left ventricle, including percutaneous alcohol septal ablation, which improves symptoms in approximately 75% to 80% of patients, or surgical septal myectomy, which improves symptoms in approximately 90% to 95% of patients. Guidelines recommend that first-degree relatives of patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy undergo screening for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with genetic testing or echocardiography.

Conclusions: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is caused by a monogenetic pathogenic variant in approximately 30% to 40% of patients and can cause effort-related dyspnea, chest pain or pressure, or lightheadedness. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is associated with an incidence of sudden cardiac death of 0.8% per year. First-line therapies for symptomatic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are β-blockers (eg, metoprolol, bisoprolol, nadolol) or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil, diltiazem).

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement and Emergency Department Visits in Opioid Use: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Individuals receiving long-term opioid therapy (LTOT) have high rates of emergency department (ED) utilization, particularly for pain, addiction, and mental health (PAMH) conditions. Behavioral interventions that reduce reliance on acute care remain limited.

Objective: To evaluate whether Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) is associated with ED utilization and ED-associated costs among veterans receiving LTOT.

Design, setting, and participants: Secondary analysis of electronic health record (EHR) data from a single-blind randomized clinical trial conducted from April 1, 2017 to October 1, 2021. Data were analyzed from March 2026 to May 2026. Participants were 185 veterans with chronic pain receiving LTOT with available EHR data.

Interventions: Participants were randomized 1 to 1 to mindfulness-oriented recovery enhancement (mindfulness, reappraisal, and savoring training) or supportive psychotherapy, each delivered in 8 two-hour group sessions.

Main outcomes and measures: ED visits and ED-related costs during months 1 through 4, 5 through 8, and 9 through 12. ED visits were identified using US Department of Veterans Affairs EHR data and classified using all available diagnosis codes; costs were estimated using national emergency department expenditure data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey. Analyses were performed from March toSeptember 2026.

Results: The sample included 185 participants (mean [SD] age, 57.5 [11.7] years; 31 women [16.8%]). During months 9 to 12, mindfulness-oriented recovery enhancement participants had 51 ED visits (0.54 visits per participant) compared with 65 ED visits (0.72 visits per participant) among supportive psychotherapy participants. Mindfulness-oriented recovery enhancement was associated with fewer ED visits during months 9 to 12 compared with supportive psychotherapy (IRR, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.13-0.65; P = .01), but not during earlier follow-ups. PAMH-associated ED visits during months 9 to 12 occurred at 0.17 visits per participant in the mindfulness-oriented recovery enhancement group compared with 0.42 visits per participant in the supportive psychotherapy group; mindfulness-oriented recovery enhancement was associated with fewer PAMH-related ED visits (IRR, 0.22; 95% CI, 0.07-0.74; P = .04). ED-associated costs during months 9 to 12 were $769.83 in the mindfulness-oriented recovery enhancement group and $1043.33 in the supportive psychotherapy group; ED-related costs were lower in the mindfulness-oriented recovery enhancement group for total ED visits and PAMH-related visits.

Conclusions and relevance: Among veterans receiving LTOT, mindfulness-oriented recovery enhancement was associated with lower ED utilization and related costs during months 9 through 12 following treatment initiation but not during earlier follow-ups. Mindfulness-oriented recovery enhancement may be associated with decreased long-term acute care utilization and should be further evaluated for its health-system impact.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: ABBV-CLS-7262 in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: ABBV-CLS-7262 is a central nervous system-penetrant eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B activator that attenuates the integrated stress response (ISR).

Objective: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of ABBV-CLS-7262 in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

Design, setting, and participants: ABBV-CLS-7262 was evaluated as a regimen of the HEALEY ALS Platform Trial, a placebo-controlled, double-blind randomized clinical trial conducted at 74 centers in the US between March 23, 2023, and October 3, 2024. Eligible participants with ALS were randomized to receive 1 of 2 doses of active drug or a matching placebo. The analysis included shared randomized participants receiving placebo from an additional regimen.

Intervention: Participants were randomized (2:1:1) to receive ABBV-CLS-7262 at a dosage of either 120 mg or 240 mg once daily or matching placebo for 24 weeks.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was rate of disease progression measured by ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised (ALSFRS-R) score and survival estimated together through a bayesian shared-parameter model relative to placebo. The primary comparison was between the 120-mg dose and placebo. The 240-mg dose was exploratory. Safety, secondary (eg, changes in ALSFRS-R total score, measures of limb and respiratory muscle strength, neurofilament light chain levels, quality of life, and cerebral spinal fluid [CSF] FGF21 levels, a putative biomarker of integrated stress response [ISR] pathway activity), and exploratory end points were also evaluated.

Results: In total, 335 participants were assigned to the ABBV-CLS-7262 regimen. Of them, 310 were randomized to receive ABBV-CLS-7262 (120-mg dose group: n = 155; 95 [61.3%] male; mean [SD] age, 57.3 [11.2] years; 240-mg dose group: n = 79; 49 [62.0%] male; mean [SD] age, 58.2 [11.0] years) and 76 to receive the regimen-specific placebo (42 [55.3%] male; mean [SD] age, 58.0 [11.1] years). An additional 50 participants were randomized to receive placebo from other concurrently enrolling regimens, bringing the total placebo group to 126 (81 [64.3%] male; mean [SD] age, 57.6 [11.7] years). Prespecified primary outcome analyses were performed comparing ABBV-CLS-7262 dose of 120 mg to the total shared placebo. The estimated median disease rate ratio common to the ALSFRS-R score and survival was 1.06 (95% credible interval, 0.85-1.32). The mean 24-week secondary outcome measures were not statistically significant between ABBV-CLS-7262 and placebo. The incidence rates of adverse events were similar between ABBV-CLS-7262 and placebo. No unexpected treatment-related risks were identified. CSF FGF21 levels decreased at week 24 in both ABBV-CLS-7262 dose groups compared with placebo (mean [SD] change from baseline, -6.8 [28.6] pg/mL for 120 mg, -8.3 [15.9] pg/mL for 240 mg, and 0.6 [11.1] pg/mL for placebo), consistent with central ISR pathway engagement and attenuation.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of ABBV-CLS-7262 in ALS, ABBV-CLS-7262 attenuated the ISR but not ALS progression. This study also provides valuable ABBV-CLS-7262 safety and tolerability data.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: State Abortion Bans and Neonatal and Infant Mortality in the US
item.description:
Importance: Following the US Supreme Court's decision in Dobbs v Jackson Women's Health Organization (hereinafter Dobbs), many states implemented abortion bans. However, evidence of a possible association between state bans and neonatal and infant mortality remains limited, with prior studies constrained by short postban follow-up periods.

Objective: To examine the association between state-level abortion bans and neonatal and infant mortality in the US.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective population-based cohort study included all 50 US states and Washington, DC, and compared 16 states that implemented abortion bans with the 34 states and Washington, DC, without bans. The National Center for Health Statistics natality and mortality data were analyzed for neonatal mortality from January 1, 2012, to December 31, 2025, and for infant mortality from January 1, 2012, to December 31, 2024, using bayesian hierarchical Poisson models with a nonnegative matrix factorization-based counterfactual framework.

Exposure: State-level implementation of complete or 6-week abortion bans.

Main outcomes and measures: Neonatal mortality (deaths before 28 days of age) and infant mortality (deaths before 1 year of age), expressed per 1000 live births.

Results: Of 52 969 264 live births from 2012 through 2025, the analysis included 198 967 neonatal deaths through 2025 and 281 873 infant deaths through 2024. Of the infant deaths, 81 860 (29.0%) occurred among Black infants, 61 356 (21.8%) among Hispanic infants, 118 707 (42.1%) among White infants, and 7.1% among infants of other racial and ethnic groups. Across 16 states with bans, neonatal mortality increased by 5.5% (95% credible interval [CrI], 2.6%-8.5%), corresponding to approximately 745 (95% CrI, 367-1139) excess neonatal deaths in the states with bans; this estimate was attenuated after excluding Texas (2.2% [95% CrI, -0.5% to 5.2%]). There was an increase in infant mortality of 1.8% (95% CrI, -0.2% to 4.3%) in the postban periods, corresponding to approximately 288 (95% CrI, -25 to 658) excess deaths; although the 95% CrI included the null, the posterior probability of a positive association was approximately 0.95. Excluding Texas attenuated this estimate to near null (0.2% [95% CrI, -1.2% to 2.0%]). Increases in infant mortality were largest among Black infants (8.8% [95% CrI, 3.3%-14.2%]) and deaths due to congenital anomalies (6.9% [95% CrI, 1.8%-12.5%]). No individual state showed a statistically credible increase in infant mortality, although neonatal mortality increases were largest and most precisely estimated in Texas.

Conclusions and relevance: In this population-based cohort study of US live births, state abortion bans were associated with an increase in neonatal mortality and with inconclusive evidence of an increase in infant mortality. Findings suggest that abortion bans contribute to widening racial disparities in neonatal and infant mortality and highlight the importance of considering downstream perinatal health effects of restrictive abortion policies.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Direct Oral Anticoagulant Use and Acute Intracranial Hemorrhage in Adults Undergoing CT After Head Injury
item.description:
Importance: Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) therapy is commonly considered a risk factor for traumatic intracranial hemorrhage after head injury, but direct comparisons with no anticoagulation exposure are limited.

Objective: To assess whether active DOAC exposure, compared with no anticoagulation exposure, is associated with acute intracranial hemorrhage among adults undergoing computed tomography (CT) imaging after head injury.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study was conducted in 3 emergency departments within a large urban National Health Service trust in London, UK. Linked emergency department, hospital, and primary care prescribing records from January 1, 2018, to December 31, 2022, were used. Adults aged 18 years or older presenting with head injury who underwent head CT were eligible. Analysis was conducted between June 2025 and June 2026.

Exposures: Active DOAC prescription (including apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban) at presentation compared with no anticoagulant prescription.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was acute intracranial hemorrhage on initial CT scan. Secondary outcomes were neurosurgical intervention and 28-day mortality. Associations were calculated using multivariable logistic regression adjusted for prespecified confounders.

Results: This study included 11 401 episodes in 10 625 unique patients (6652 male [58.3%]; median age, 52 years [IQR, 33-77 years]). A total of 565 episodes (5.0%) occurred in participants prescribed DOAC therapy, and 10 836 episodes (95.0%) occurred in those with no anticoagulant exposure. Acute intracranial hemorrhage occurred in 40 DOAC-treated episodes (7.1%) and 831 non-anticoagulant-treated episodes (7.7%). After adjustment, DOAC exposure was not associated with acute intracranial hemorrhage (adjusted odds ratio [AOR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.70-1.21). Neurosurgical intervention occurred in 2 DOAC-treated episodes and 44 non-anticoagulant-treated episodes (0.4% in each group, AOR, 1.58; 95% CI, 0.47-4.17). Although crude 28-day mortality was higher among DOAC-treated episodes (17 of 565 [3.0%] vs 185 of 10 836 [1.7%]), adjusted analyses did not show higher odds of mortality (AOR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.46-1.01).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of adults undergoing CT imaging after head injury, DOAC exposure was not associated with higher adjusted odds of acute intracranial hemorrhage, neurosurgical intervention, or 28-day mortality compared with no anticoagulant exposure. However, clinically important differences cannot be excluded.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Cardiovascular Risk Factors and Biomarkers in the Decades Prior to a Cardiovascular Event
item.description:
Importance: Prior studies on trajectories of risk factors have typically focused on a single marker or did not study trajectories in association with cardiovascular events.

Objective: To evaluate sex- and age-specific trajectories of cardiovascular risk factors and circulating biomarkers associated with cardiovascular events and over the adult life course.

Design, setting, and participants: Longitudinal individual participant data from 4 cohort studies (Cardiovascular Health Study, Trøndelag Health Study, Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, and Whitehall II) were pooled, covering a 34-year period (1985-2019). Analyses were conducted from April 2025 to September 2026.

Exposures: Repeatedly measured cardiovascular risk factors and circulating biomarkers (C-reactive protein, cardiac troponins, and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was a composite of first-onset nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or cardiovascular death. Linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models were used to estimate trajectories across individuals who experienced the primary outcome and those who survived and did not experience the primary outcome.

Results: In total, there were 316 719 study visits for 113 612 individuals without prior myocardial infarction or stroke, including 59 328 female individuals (52.2%; median [IQR] age at inclusion, 46 [33-61] years) and 54 284 male individuals (47.8%; median [IQR] age at inclusion, 45 [35-58] years). The primary outcome occurred in 8025 female individuals (13.5%) and 8892 male individuals (16.4%) during a median (IQR) follow-up of 18.9 (10.2-27.4) years. Individuals who experienced the primary outcome had less favorable cardiovascular risk factor trajectories and greater cumulative exposure than those who remained event free, with divergence evident up to 3 decades before the event. For instance, systolic blood pressure among female individuals was 4 mm Hg higher 3 decades before the event (121 mm Hg [95% CI, 119-123 mm Hg] vs 117 mm Hg [95% CI, 117-117 mm Hg]) and 7 mm Hg higher at time of the event or censoring (137 mm Hg [95% CI, 136-139 mm Hg] vs 130 mm Hg [95% CI, 129-130 mm Hg]). Similar long-term differences were observed in male individuals and for other cardiovascular risk factors. Cardiovascular biomarker trajectories began to diverge 1 to 3 decades before the event. For instance, differences in N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide concentrations became apparent 1 decade before the event in both female (0.18 [95% CI, 0.07-0.30] SD log2 difference) and male (0.32 [95% CI, 0.21-0.42] SD log2 difference) individuals.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of individuals free from cardiovascular disease at baseline, trajectories of cardiovascular risk factors and biomarkers diverged between individuals who experienced the event and those who remained event free up to 3 decades before first-onset cardiovascular disease. These findings highlight the potential for earlier, life-course prevention strategies.

Over 4 years of follow-up, 156 programs responded to the implementation assessments; 123 (70.3%) reported active use, including 80 (45.7%) using the PDA as standard of care and 23 (13.1%) using it frequently. Overall, 7132 patients received the PDA, representing 83.2% of eligible patients at participating programs. Common barriers included limited implementation capacity or preference for existing materials.

Conclusions and relevance: This nationwide quality improvement study of LVAD medical decision-making found that 70.3% of all LVAD programs in the US reported using a proven effective PDA with their patients. Importance: A multidimensional chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) diagnostic schema incorporating imaging and clinical features beyond airflow obstruction has been proposed. Objective: To compare the population-level classification and prognostic implications of a multidimensional COPD diagnostic schema with those of the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) definition.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based cohort study used the Swedish Cardiopulmonary Bioimage Study, conducted at 6 Swedish university hospitals 2013-2018 to compare diagnostic definitions in the full cohort and in a symptom-restricted subgroup approximating routine clinical practice, with mortality follow-up through September 30, 2024. Randomly sampled adults aged 50 to 64 years with complete classification data, including postbronchodilator spirometry and chest computed tomography assessment of emphysema and bronchial wall thickening were included.

Exposure: Classification according to the multidimensional COPD diagnostic schema and an operationalized GOLD definition.

Main outcomes and measures: COPD prevalence, case composition, and all-cause mortality.

Results: A total of 29 281 participants (15011 females [51.3%]; mean [SD] age, 57.5 [4.3] years) were included; 1347 participants (4.6%) met multidimensional COPD criteria. In analyses restricted to 6016 symptomatic individuals, prevalence was similar under the multidimensional and GOLD definitions (909 [15.1%] vs 853 [14.2%]), but case composition differed. Approximately one-third of patients with multidimensional COPD (281 of 909 [30.9%]) did not meet the GOLD criteria. Across the full cohort, 438 individuals (32.5% of multidimensional COPD cases) were asymptomatic and would be unlikely to undergo diagnostic evaluation in routine symptom-driven care. During follow-up, 634 deaths occurred. Among symptomatic participants, adjusted mortality risk was increased in multidimensional-only cases (hazard ratio [HR], 2.58; 95% CI, 1.66-4.01) and those meeting both definitions (HR, 2.20; 95% CI, 1.59-3.04), but not in patients with GOLD-only COPD (HR, 0.94; 95% CI, 0.44-2.00).

Conclusions and relevance: In this population-based cohort study, COPD prevalence was similar with a multidimensional COPD diagnostic schema to that obtained using GOLD criteria, but case composition differed substantially. The multidimensional schema identified increased mortality risk among individuals not captured by GOLD, suggesting improved prognostic stratification, while the identification of many asymptomatic cases highlights an existing detection gap in current symptom-driven care pathways.

item.title: Intensive Care Med: Subphenotyping and precision medicine approaches to ARDS
item.description:
Sixty years after its initial description, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) remains defined by bilateral radiographic opacities and impaired oxygenation rather than by its underlying biology. This syndromic definition encompasses considerable clinical and biological heterogeneity, which may contribute to the ineffectiveness of pharmacotherapy trials to date. Subphenotyping aims to address this heterogeneity by identifying more homogeneous patient groups that differ in prognosis and/or treatment response. In this narrative review, framed by the research questions outlined in the 2023 European Society of Intensive Care Medicine guidelines, we synthesize current approaches to ARDS subphenotyping across complementary domains: clinical (etiology, rapidly improving ARDS), physiological (gas exchange, recruitability, elastance, and ventilatory ratio), morphological (focal versus non-focal radiological patterns), and biological (individual injury biomarkers and the hyperinflammatory and hypoinflammatory subphenotypes). We examine their pathobiological basis, temporal dynamics, and retrospective evidence for heterogeneity of treatment effect, and consider how parsimonious biomarker panels, machine-learning classifiers, and adaptive basket trial designs may support clinical implementation. Prospective validation across diverse populations, including resource-limited settings, remains a key priority.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Long-Term Cognitive Function Following Haloperidol Vs. Placebo Treatment in ICU Patients With Delirium
item.description:
Objective: To investigate the effects of haloperidol vs. placebo on long-term cognitive function in formerly critically ill patients with ICU delirium, 1 year after randomization in the Agents Intervening against Delirium in the ICU (AID-ICU) randomized clinical trial.

Design: Pre-planned 1-year follow-up of the AID-ICU trial conducted from June 2019 to April 2023.

Setting: Three university-affiliated ICUs in Denmark.

Patients: Adult ICU patients previously enrolled in the AID-ICU trial.

Interventions: Patients in the AID-ICU were randomized to either haloperidol or placebo (0.9% saline) when treated for delirium in the ICU.

Measurements and main results: The primary outcome was global cognitive function at 1 year, assessed using Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychologic Status (RBANS) Global Index Score Secondary outcomes including domain-specific RBANS scores and executive function, measured by the Trail Making Test A and B. Analyses used the intention-to-treat population. Non-survivors were assigned the lowest possible score on each outcome, reflecting death as a competing outcome. Missing data among survivors were handled using multiple imputations. Of the 632 randomized patients, 624 were included. Cognitive outcome data were available for 134 of 343 surviving patients: 67 in the haloperidol group and 67 in the placebo group. Median global cognitive scores were 40 (interquartile range [IQR]: 40-75) in the haloperidol group and 40 (IQR: 40-72) in the placebo group (mean difference: 2; 95% CI, -3 to 7; p = 0.48). No significant differences were observed in secondary outcomes. Given the high proportion of missing data, best-worst and worst-best sensitivity analyses were performed, yielding estimates in opposite directions.

Conclusions: In this 1-year follow-up of the AID-ICU treatment with haloperidol for delirium in the ICU was not associated with improved long-term cognitive function compared with placebo. However, given the extent of missing outcome data and the divergent results of our sensitivity analyses, this estimate should be interpreted as imprecise rather than conclusive; clinically relevant effects of pharmacologic delirium treatment on cognition cannot be excluded, and future adequately powered studies with more complete follow-up are warranted.

item.title: Am J Respir Crit Care Med: Multidimensional Predictors of Post-Traumatic Stress in Relatives of Critically Ill Patients
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Relatives of critically ill patients frequently develop post-traumatic stress symptoms. Few studies have evaluated both psychological and ICU-related risk factors.

Objectives: We aimed to identify factors associated with post-traumatic stress symptom severity and probable post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in ICU relatives.

Methods: In this prospective multicentre cohort study (FAME), we enrolled consecutive adults on mechanical ventilation for ≥48 h in 60 ICUs in France (15 December 2022-30 January 2024); for each patient, we enrolled one relative. The relatives completed validated instruments during the ICU stay and follow-up interviews at three and six months. The primary outcome was higher PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 [PCL-5] at 3 months. Associations were sought using multivariable logistic regression for PCL-5 scores ≥31 and multivariable linear regression for three-month PCL-5 scores.

Measurements and main results: Of 1346 relatives, 936 (69·5%) completed PCL-5 at 3-month: 106 (11·3%) had probable PTSD and 358 (38·2%) clinically relevant post-traumatic stress symptoms. Factors associated with higher PCL-5 scores included pre-existing characteristics (social exclusion, living alone, perceived disability, and history of psychological trauma), early symptoms (anxiety, peritraumatic dissociation, and insomnia), and greater severity in the patients (vasopressor use and end-of-life decisions). Lower PCL-5 scores were associated with male sex and specific physician communication behaviours.

Conclusion: Post-traumatic stress symptoms were common, and approximately one in nine relatives had probable PTSD at three months. Knowledge of early psychological markers may help identify relatives at risk, while improved communication practices may decrease the risk.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: A community-led compassion club as an alternative to illicit drug markets: Pricing and changes in high-intensity drug use
item.description:
Objectives: In 2022, the Drug User Liberation Front (DULF) began operating a non-medicalized safer supply compassion club (CC) where members could purchase rigorously tested illicit cocaine, heroin and methamphetamine at cost. The present study sought to compare DULF CC drug prices with local street prices and examine the association between enrollment in the DULF CC and high-intensity drug use.

Methods: An economic analysis compared the prices of DULF CC drugs with prevailing street-market prices reported by participants in the Vancouver Injection Drug Users Study (VIDUS), a community-recruited prospective cohort of people who use drugs in Vancouver. Generalized estimating equation (GEE) logistic regression analyses were used to examine the association between CC enrollment and self-reported high-intensity (≥daily vs. <daily) use of methamphetamine, cocaine and opioids, respectively, among a prospective cohort of DULF CC participants.

Results: During the August 2022 to October 2023 study period, DULF CC drugs were found to be consistently less expensive and less variable in price than their street-market counterparts. In multivariable GEE analyses, enrollment in the DULF CC was associated with significantly lower odds of high-intensity methamphetamine use (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] = 0.49, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.29-0.82; p = 0.007) and high-intensity opioid use (AOR = 0.56, 95% CI: 0.37-0.85; p = 0.006), while no significant association was observed for high-intensity cocaine use.

Discussion: Findings suggest that the DULF CC provided community-regulated drugs at lower and more stable prices than those available through illicit markets, and that enrollment was associated with reductions in opioid and methamphetamine use.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Social control of cocaine intake: Sex differences in behavioral vs. cocaine-exposure cues
item.description:
Background: Drug taking is influenced by social partners, but the social cues that control another individual's drug use remain unclear.

Objective: The present study determined whether cocaine self-administration is influenced more by a partner's level of cocaine-maintained responding or by the partner's level of cocaine intake.

Methods: Male and female rats were assigned to same-sex observer-model dyads. Following initial cocaine self-administration training, observer rats self-administered 0.3mg/kg/infusion cocaine under a fixed-ratio 1 schedule throughout testing. One group of models self-administered cocaine under individualized variable-ratio (VR) schedules that maintained high rates of lever pressing, with each model tested at 0.1, 0.3, and 1.0mg/kg/infusion. A second group received cocaine noncontingently (NT) and was yoked to the VR models, receiving the same number and timing of cocaine infusions without lever pressing.

Results: Observer responding varied as a function of model schedule, cocaine dose, and sex. In male observer rats, responding followed an inverted-U-shaped function across model dose in the VR condition, closely paralleling partner lever pressing, but remained unchanged across dose in the NT condition. In contrast, female observer responding increased with model cocaine dose under both VR and NT conditions, paralleling partner cocaine intake.

Conclusions: These findings indicate that features of a cocaine-using social partner can differentially influence cocaine self-administration in male and female rats. Under these conditions, the responding of male observers was more strongly controlled by the partner's level of cocaine-maintained responding, whereas the responding of female observers was more closely related to the partner's level of cocaine intake.

item.title: Chest: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing responses to treatment in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension and cardiopulmonary comorbidities
item.description:
Background: Current ESC/ERS guidelines suggest that initial monotherapy should be considered for pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) with cardiopulmonary comorbidities. However, data on the cardiopulmonary physiological responses to treatment in this subset of patients remain limited. Our aim was to evaluate the cardiopulmonary exercise and gas exchange response to treatment in patients with PAH and cardiopulmonary comorbidities.

Research question: Do patients with PAH and a cardiopulmonary phenotype display a worse exercise capacity and gas exchange response to treatment?

Study design and methods: Incident treatment-naïve patients with idiopathic, heritable, drug/toxins-induced, HIV, and connective tissue disease-associated PAH were analysed at first follow-up. Comorbid patients were defined based on the presence of ≥3 risk factors among obesity (body mass index ≥30 Kg/m2), systemic arterial hypertension, diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, smoking history and transfer factor of the lung for carbon monoxide (TLCO) <45% predicted.

Results: A total of 178 patients were included: 52 with comorbidities and 126 without. Comorbid patients were older, predominantly male, and had a lower baseline exercise capacity, despite comparable hemodynamics. There were no differences in therapy, with approximately one third of patients receiving combination therapy in both groups at the time of reassessment. At follow-up, both groups demonstrated similar adjusted improvements from baseline in peak oxygen uptake, oxygen pulse, ventilatory efficiency and 6-minute walk distance, all known prognostic markers in PAH. However, comorbid patients exhibited a significantly worse gas exchange response to treatment, with an adjusted widening of the peak A-a gradient of +1.23 kPa compared with -0.35 kPa in patients without comorbidities (p=0.003).

Interpretation: PAH patients with and without cardiopulmonary comorbidities achieve similar improvements in exercise capacity after treatment. However, the worse gas exchange response to exercise among comorbid patients warrants caution, careful monitoring and further research to confirm this finding.

item.title: Chest: Real-World Outcomes of Long-Acting Beta-Agonist Add-On Therapy to Inhaled Corticosteroids in Preschool Children with Asthma: A Multicenter Retrospective Study
item.description:
Background: The role of long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) add-on therapy to inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) in preschool children with asthma remains uncertain. Although ICS+LABA is an established step-up strategy, data in children younger than 6 years are limited.

Research question: In children ≤6 years with asthma, how were morbidity outcomes associated with ICS+LABA therapy compared with ICS alone, before and after LABA initiation?

Study design: and Methods: This retrospective comparative effectiveness study used the TriNetX research network, a multicenter electronic health record database. Children aged ≤6 years with asthma treated with ICS+LABA were compared with propensity-matched children treated with ICS alone (n≈12,100 per cohort). To account for treatment timing and the age-related effects on asthma severity and incidence, analyses were conducted using two index definitions: asthma diagnosis with LABA initiation within 12 months, and the time of LABA initiation itself. Outcomes included systemic corticosteroid exposure, bronchodilator use, ED visits/hospitalizations, pneumonia, fractures, and gastroenteritis.

Results: When indexed at asthma diagnosis, ICS+LABA was associated with higher hazards of systemic corticosteroid exposure (HR, 1.37; 95% CI, 1.32-1.43), bronchodilator use (HR, 1.41; 95% CI, 1.36-1.46), and pneumonia (HR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.28-1.52) compared to ICS alone. When reindexed to LABA initiation, these associations were attenuated, but not eliminated: systemic corticosteroid exposure (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.09-1.18), bronchodilator use (HR, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.13-1.21), and pneumonia (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.02-1.22). Direct comparison of the ICS+LABA cohort across index definitions showed lower rates of asthma-related outcomes after LABA initiation. Findings were similar in unmatched analyses, and in sensitivity analyses by younger age, later follow-up, Bayesian analysis and LABA type.

Interpretation: In young children selected for ICS+LABA escalation, excess morbidity was greatest compared to ICS alone before LABA initiation and attenuated after LABA initiation. These findings may provide real-world evidence for ICS+LABA effectiveness in a selected group of preschool children with uncontrolled asthma and the basis for future prospective studies.

item.title: Chest: Association between exertional dyspnea and insomnia in a population-based cohort
item.description:
Background: Dyspnea is unexplained in 15% of patients. Insomnia has been associated with respiratory diseases, but its relationship with dyspnea in general population remains uncertain.

Research question: Is there an association between dyspnea and insomnia, defined according to different criteria, using data from a population-based cohort?

Study design and methods: Participants underwent complete respiratory, psychiatric and sleep assessments. Dyspnea (dependent variable) was defined as modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) ≥ 1. Insomnia (independent variable) was defined with Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) cut-offs ≥8 or ≥15, and with ISI categories as subthreshold (ISI 8 to 14) or clinical (ISI≥15) insomnia. Logistic regressions were performed adjusted for age, sex, BMI, smoking, FEV1, AHI, psychiatric disorders and self-reported cardiac and respiratory disorders. We defined unexplained dyspnea with mMRC≥1 for participants of a healthy group (normal spirometry, normal Nt-proBNP, no anemia, no respiratory or cardiac disorders and normal electrocardiogram).

Results: We included 1'221 participants (mean age 62.2 years; female 52%) of whom 42% reported dyspnea and 18% reported insomnia (ISI≥8). The prevalence of dyspnea increased among ISI categories. After adjustment, higher odds of dyspnea were significantly associated with ISI cut-offs ≥ 8 (OR 1.87, CI95 1.31-2.67) and ≥ 15 (OR 1.96, CI95 1.09-3.64), as well as subthreshold insomnia (OR 1.76, CI95 1.17-2.64) and clinical insomnia (OR 2.17, CI95 1.16-4.05), all FDR p-value<0.05. Unexplained dyspnea was also associated with ISI≥8.

item.title: Chest: Combination acetazolamide and supplemental oxygen markedly improves ventilatory control instability and OSA severity
item.description:
Introduction: Ventilatory control instability (elevated 'loop gain') is a key pathophysiological determinant of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but available interventions have modest potency.

Research question: Since acetazolamide (ACZ) and supplemental oxygen (O2) independently lower loop gain via different mechanisms, can combination ACZO2 strongly reduce loop gain and therefore OSA severity?

Study design and method: In a randomized, single-blind, crossover trial, 22 participants with moderate-severe OSA (15 M, 7 F), received ACZ (500 mg daily) or placebo for 7 days. On the final nights of each period, participants underwent two nights of polysomnography with O2 (3 L/min) or sham. Loop gain (LG1) and flow-based apnea-hypopnea-index (fAHI, events scored without desaturation/arousal criteria) were assessed from polysomnography at each visit.

Results: Compared with placebo+sham both ACZ and O2 monotherapies produced significant reduction in both LG1 and AHI. Combination ACZO2 markedly reduced LG1 by -0.26 [CI95%: -0.32, -0.20], and further significantly reduced LG1 compared to both ACZ (-0.07 [-0.13, -0.01]) and O2 alone -0.08 [-0.14, -0.02]. ACZO2 strongly reduced fAHI by -23.3/hr [-26.6, -13.1] (-55.2% [-63.9, -44.4]), however was not superior to ACZ alone (-3.4/h [-8.5, 1.6], -14.6% [-31.1, 5.8]).

Interpretation: In patients with OSA, combining acetazolamide and supplemental oxygen provides a potent reduction in loop gain and roughly halves the AHI. This combination intervention holds promise for individuals whose OSA is meaningfully driven by elevated ventilatory control.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: The role of early school performance on subsequent alcohol and drug use disorders: A Swedish cohort study
item.description:
Aims: To examine whether lower academic performance in compulsory school (age 15-16) increases the risk of later alcohol use disorder (AUD) and drug use disorder (DUD), and to assess the extent to which shared familial factors account for these associations.

Methods: This national cohort study included 2937,919 individuals born in Sweden between 1972 and 2002, residing in Sweden on 1 July of the year in which school grades were assessed (ages 15-16 years), followed until first diagnosis of AUD without comorbid DUD, DUD without comorbid AUD, death, or December 31, 2023. Academic performance was measured using 9th-grade grade point average and categorized into deciles. Cox proportional hazards models estimated hazard ratios (HRs), and sibling-comparison models were used to adjust for shared familial genetic and environmental factors FINDINGS: Lower academic performance was strongly associated with increased risk of both AUD and DUD, showing a clear dose-response pattern across the full grade distribution. Risks were consistently higher for DUD than for AUD, and the associations remained robust in sibling-comparison analyses, although somewhat attenuated.

Conclusion: Lower academic performance in adolescence is a strong predictor of later AUD and DUD, with markedly higher risks for DUD. Neither birth year, sex, maternal and paternal psychiatric history, parental income, nor the highest parental education origin, nor shared familial factors fully explain the association.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Comparative effectiveness and safety of generic versus brand-name varenicline for smoking cessation in Chinese population: Findings from China National Tobacco Cessation Cohort Study (CNTCCS)
item.description:
Background: Following the global withdrawal of brand-name varenicline due to nitrosamine contamination, generic formulations have become the only available varenicline option for smoking cessation in China. To compare the real-world effectiveness and safety of generic versus brand-name varenicline for smoking cessation in China.

Methods: We conducted a nationwide, multicenter, historical-comparator cohort analysis using data from the China National Tobacco Cessation Cohort Study (CNTCCS). The primary outcome was biochemically validated 7-day point prevalence abstinence at 24 weeks. Secondary outcomes included continuous abstinence, medication adherence, and adverse reactions. A modified Intention-to-treat analyses were performed.

Results: Among 1209 participants, 256 initiated generic varenicline and 953 initiated brand-name varenicline; 512 participants were included after matching. At 24 weeks, validated abstinence rates were similar between generic and brand-name varenicline both before matching (33.2% vs. 33.8%) and after matching (33.2% vs. 33.2%). Medication adherence declined over time in both groups and was comparable throughout follow-up (all P > 0.05). However, adverse reactions were more frequently reported with generic varenicline (32.4% vs. 12.1% at week 1; 18.0% vs. 7.0% at week 12; all P < 0.001), although no serious adverse events occurred in either group.

Conclusions: In this historical-comparator cohort analysis, generic and brand-name varenicline demonstrated similar smoking cessation effectiveness at 24 weeks. Generic varenicline was associated with a higher frequency of nonserious adverse reactions, highlighting the importance of monitoring tolerability in routine clinical practice. These findings support the continued use of generic varenicline for smoking cessation following the withdrawal of the brand-name product.

item.title: Crit Care: Predictive performance of bedside physiological parameters for the failure of prophylactic non-invasive ventilation after extubation
item.description:
Background: Extubation failure is associated with increased mortality. Whether bedside physiological variables can identify patients at risk of reintubation during prophylactic NIV after extubation is unknown.

Methods: In this post hoc analysis of a multicenter physiological study, 60 hypoxemic adults at high risk of extubation failure underwent two 1-hour NIV sessions after planned extubation, with oronasal and full-face masks in randomized crossover order. We assessed the magnitude of airway occlusion pressure (Pocc), the esophageal pressure swing (ΔPes), SpO₂/FiO₂, respiratory rate, tidal volume, dynamic lung elastance (EL,dyn), ROX index [(SpO₂/FiO₂)/respiratory rate] and the pressure-oxygenation index (POX, SpO₂/FiO₂ divided by Pocc). Prophylactic NIV failure was reintubation for respiratory failure within 7 days. Discrimination was assessed by ROC analysis.

Results: Fourteen patients (23%) experienced NIV failure. Pocc yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.83 (95% CI, 0.71-0.95) with the oronasal mask and 0.83 (95% CI, 0.72-0.95) with the full-face mask, showing greater discriminative performance than tidal volume (AUCs, 0.55 and 0.53), respiratory rate (0.54 and 0.38), SpO₂/FiO₂ (0.51 and 0.50), and the ROX index (0.54 and 0.38; all p < 0.05). By contrast, the discriminative performance of Pocc did not differ from that of EL,dyn (AUCs, 0.72 and 0.73; p = 0.08 and 0.11), POX (AUCs, 0.82 and 0.81; p = 0.68 and 0.29), or |ΔPes| (AUCs, 0.83 and 0.82; p = 1.00 and 0.64).

Conclusions: During prophylactic NIV, Pocc discriminated NIV failure better than conventional bedside variables, with no detectable difference from directly measured inspiratory effort. External validation is required.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Prehospital Trauma Compendium: Prehospital Management of Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Circulatory Arrest - A Joint Position Statement and Resource Document of NAEMSP, ACS-COT, ACEP, and AAP
item.description:
In 2014 the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP), American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma (ACS-COT), American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) published the first joint position statement discussing withholding and discontinuing resuscitation attempts for pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital circulatory arrest (TOHCA). Since then, the body of literature addressing pediatric TOHCA has evolved and evidence has grown that demonstrates the nearly uniformly poor prognosis of children who suffer circulatory arrest in the prehospital setting as a result of trauma. To support emergency medical services (EMS) clinicians in their approach to these high-acuity, low-frequency, and challenging cases, this project aimed to update guidance regarding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts for pediatric traumatic circulatory arrest. NAEMSP, ACEP, ACS-COT, and AAP recommend:EMS resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA should:Prioritize prompt identification of patients who may benefit from transport to definitive care at trauma centers when safe and appropriate. On-scene resuscitation should be balanced against the potential benefit of transfer to a proximate trauma center.Emphasize the identification of reversible causes of traumatic circulatory arrest and timely use of clinically indicated life-saving interventions (LSIs) within the EMS clinician's scope of practice. These include:External hemorrhage control with direct pressure, wound packing, and tourniquetsAirway management using the least-invasive airway interventions required to achieve and maintain airway patency, oxygenation, and adequate ventilation.Chest decompression if clinical concern for tension pneumothorax. Empiric bilateral decompression is not recommended in the absence of suspected thoracic trauma.External chest compressions and ventilations have a larger role in pediatric TOHCA resuscitation than in adult TOHCA resuscitation, with children frequently having TOHCA secondary to head injury, hypoxia and other non-hemorrhagic mechanisms. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) should be provided when the cause of circulatory arrest is unclear.Epinephrine is of lower priority than other LSIs.Consider point of care ultrasound (POCUS) to guide decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation efforts.Resuscitation attempts may be withheld in pediatric TOHCA patients with:Injuries that are incompatible with life (e.g., decapitation, hemi-corpectomy, incineration).Evidence of prolonged circulatory arrest (e.g., rigor mortis, dependent lividity, decomposition).Advanced care planning documents that indicate Do Not Resuscitate (DNR)/ Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR)/Allow Natural Death medical orders.Resuscitation attempts may be discontinued in pediatric TOHCA patients who:Have no return of spontaneous circulation after provision of at least 15 minutes of high-quality CPR in addition to performance of other lifesaving interventions directed at treating potentially reversible causes of pediatric TOHCA. Longer durations of CPR, up to 30 minutes, may be considered for patients with positive predictors of survival such as organized rhythm, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, or with proximate access to a trauma center.Have known predictors of very low probability of survival such as penetrating trauma without proximate access to a trauma center, asystole, unwitnessed arrest, or lack of bystander CPR.Protocols guiding decisions to withhold or discontinue resuscitation of pediatric TOHCA benefit from oversight by EMS physicians in collaboration with pediatric experts and local or regional trauma system stakeholders. Implementation of such protocols for pediatric patients benefits from involvement of community stakeholders including family representatives, law enforcement, medical examiner, and child fatality review committees.Considerations for protocol implementation include local resource availability, EMS clinician and public safety, psychosocial support to surviving family members and emergency responders, and dignified handling of the deceased patient.Training needs for EMS clinicians include techniques to communicate with family members regarding the death of a child and understanding the clinician's own response to this low-frequency, high-emotion experience.

item.title: Crit Care Med: Prevalence and Characteristics of Coma in Latin American Critical Care Units: The COMA LATAM Study
item.description:
Objectives: To determine the point prevalence of coma across Latin American critical care units, characterize its etiology, and explore short-term outcomes.

Design: Multinational, cross-sectional point prevalence study with exploratory 14-day follow-up assessment.

Setting: Three hundred ninety-two hospitals across 19 Latin American countries, including ICUs, intermediate care units, neurocritical care units, cardiovascular ICUs, and trauma ICUs.

Patients: Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) meeting the Coma Epidemiology, Evaluation, and Therapy care survey (COME-TOGETHER) criteria on May 28, 2024. Patients under deep sedation or pharmacological coma induction were excluded unless the coma state preceded pharmacological intervention.

Interventions: None (observational study).

Measurements and main results: Among 8305 critically ill patients, 1145 met coma criteria (point prevalence 13.8%), with country-specific rates ranging from 5.1% to 36.8%. Individual patient data were available for 729 patients (63.7%). Traumatic brain injury was the leading individual cause (24.8%), followed by hypoxic-anoxic brain injury (14.6%) and intracerebral hemorrhage (13.5%). When categorized by pathophysiology, vascular causes predominated (48.6%), followed by traumatic brain injury (24.8%) and other causes (26.6%). Age-stratified analysis revealed trauma predominantly affecting younger patients, while cerebrovascular causes predominated in older groups. Among patients with 14-day follow-up data (29% of cohort), mortality was 29.2%, with 67.7% of survivors recovering from coma. Only the Charlson Comorbidity Index was independently associated with implementation of life-sustaining therapy limitations (adjusted odds ratio, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.15-1.30; p < 0.001).

Conclusions: Coma affects nearly one in seven ICU beds across Latin America, with substantial country variation and distinct age-dependent etiology patterns. The significant burden highlights the need for targeted prevention strategies and specialized neurocritical care resources throughout the region.

item.title: Am J Respir Crit Care Med: Charcot-Leyden crystals drive a localized inflammatory niche around mucus plugs in Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis
item.category: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
item.description:
Rationale: Mucus plugging causes airflow obstruction, morbidity, and mortality in chronic respiratory diseases. Charcot-Leyden crystals (CLCs), formed from eosinophil-derived Galectin-10, are frequently observed in pathologic mucus, but their role in disease is unclear.

Objectives: To define the prevalence, inflammatory context, and functional role of CLCs in mucus plugs, using acute allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) as a model of eosinophilic muco-obstructive disease.

Methods: Airway samples from 19 patients with acute ABPA and 61 disease controls were analyzed for CLCs and Galectin-10. Paired samples from plugged and unplugged bronchial mucosal biopsies defined the spatial relationship between CLCs and inflammation. A novel mouse model demonstrated the contribution of CLCs to airway obstruction and inflammation and enabled evaluation of CLC-directed imaging and therapy.

Measurements and main results: Airway CLCs were a sensitive and specific marker of acute ABPA. CLC-containing mucus plugs were surrounded by a localized type 2 inflammatory niche, alongside eosinophils, neutrophils and extracellular traps, whereas inflammation was minimal in unplugged airways from the same patients, or plugs lacking CLCs. In mice, CLC-containing plugs induced persistent airway obstruction and local inflammation, both reduced by a crystal-dissolving anti-Galectin-10 antibody. Galectin-10 concentrations provided a quantitative biomarker of acute ABPA, while a CLC-targeted positron emission tomography tracer enabled noninvasive visualization of crystal-rich plugs.

Conclusions: CLC-containing mucus plugs form focal inflammatory niches in acute ABPA, and experimental CLC deposition is sufficient to promote persistent airway obstruction and inflammation. These findings identify CLCs as a biomarker, imaging target, and tractable therapeutic target in eosinophilic muco-obstructive airway disease.
